articles.title: House speaker sending lawmakers home early ahead of US midterm election recess
articles.summary: Mike Johnson cancels votes on Thursday, meaning House members will avoid voting on impeaching Pete Hegseth
articles.byline: Ariana Baio in New York and Shrai Popat in Washington

blocks.text: The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess.

The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence.

It’s the latest round of cancelations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday.

“I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican Party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” Democratic rep Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch.

Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump.

“We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” the House speaker told reporters on Tuesday. “Because then we will lose our edge to China, and ​that has serious national security implications for every American family.”
More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson, via a letter, to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to vote on the AI safeguards.
The Guardian has asked Johnson’s office for comment.
In a notice on Wednesday, House leadership told members that other votes on EPA regulations, originally planned for Thursday, would instead take place Wednesday afternoon.

articles.title: Labour holds No 10 drinks party for donors amid growing calls for donations cap
articles.summary:
Labour has also increased fundraising from members in response to Reform’s £72m donations from crypto billionaires

Labour has hosted major party donors at No 10 for a drinks reception, as…

blocks.text: Labour has hosted major party donors at No 10 for a drinks reception, as the party comes under growing pressure from MPs and unions to consider a donations cap.

The Guardian understands that high-level donors, including business leaders and philanthropists, were hosted by cabinet ministers in Downing Street for an evening reception on Tuesday. Donors from the party’s Rose Network give thousands of pounds a year to the party.

Andy Burnham is under increased pressure from MPs to consider new restrictions for domestic donors after Reform UK received £72m from two cryptobillionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, over the course of 48 hours. A Labour source said the donors event had been organised in advance of the Reform donations news.

Over the weekend, Labour also stepped up fundraising from members, directly in response to the donations. The party’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, sent out two fundraising emails – understood to have both raised significant sums – calling on members to step up.

The Labour email said Reform had secured “record-breaking financial backing – but for us it has to be a call to action … We cannot let less than a handful of extraordinarily wealthy crypto-billionaires simply drown Labour’s message out in elections to come [with] Reform dominating what voters see and hear, Labour fighting to be heard.”
The follow-up email had a message from Phillipson saying: “When I saw that two crypto-billionaires had given Reform £72m, I had the same thought you probably did: how do you compete with that?

“Then I watched the response from Labour supporters. People donated what they could … One person can’t match £72m. But thousands of us, standing together, can make sure Labour is as well-resourced for the fight ahead as it is possible to be.”
On Tuesday, trade union leaders at the TUC stopped short of backing a cap on political donations, but called for further action on big money in politics.

General secretaries have been split on a call for unions to back a specific cap on individual donors to political parties while protecting trade union donations, which the TUC said were the “cleanest money in politics” because they came from workers’ subscriptions.
The TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said the donations to Reform were “a blatant attempt to effect a corporate takeover of our politics” and this should “ring alarm bells”.
Downing Street, however, will take some succour from the warmer tone of union chiefs towards the party leadership at the annual TUC gathering in Brighton this week.
Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from affiliated trade unions, which raise their money through individual workers’ membership fees.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, who had previously threatened to break the link with Labour, said Andy Burnham had earned the party a “second hearing”.
Several other union leaders spoke of warm chats with the prime minister since he took office, and felt they were getting more of a hearing than when Keir Starmer was in No 10.

However, despite welcoming the “Burnham bounce”, which they saw as giving Labour a better chance of fighting off the Reform threat, they warned there were key tests ahead for the government, including at the budget.
Labour is under significant financial pressure, especially after several byelections, including the Greater Manchester mayoralty.

Its most recent accounts filed with the Electoral Commission show Labour has lost more than a fifth of its membership in the space of a year, though party sources have said membership had gone up in anticipation of a possible leadership election, and since Burnham became prime minister.

Income from donations has dropped by 84% since the election year, a drop that would be expected but is still significant. Last year, the party reported a £2.6m deficit. One union leader said the party was still “millions” in the red.

However, Labour’s outgoing general secretary, Hollie Ridley, was understood to have told the party’s governing national executive committee that finances were healthy. She said the party was in its strongest financial position since the general election, due to spending discipline and increased fundraising efforts.

articles.title: Reader Q&A: how united are the Democrats ahead of the US midterms? Live now
articles.summary: Who are the Democrats running in the midterms, and where do they stand? Our US political reporters are live now to discuss the state of the Democrats, the party’s moderate and leftwing candidates…
articles.byline: Shrai Popat, David Smith, Alice Speri, Joseph Gedeon and Rachel Leingang

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1m agoWill the Democratic voters still ‘vote blue’ regardless of the candidate?
8m agoWhat should the primary focus be for Democrats if they win?
14m agoCan being too united be a bad thing?
21m agoWhat are the races to watch to understand the state of the Democrats?
28m agoWill the Democrats consolidate the way Republicans did around Trump?
18h agoWelcome to the Conversation

blocks.text: Will the Democratic voters still ‘vote blue’ regardless of the candidate?

Puttyinhishand asks: Will the “campaign/vote blue regardless of the candidate” mantra – which the Democrat left has been bludgeoned with for years – be actively honoured by the DNC and other party centrists if DSA candidates have won primaries?

double quotation markRachel: So far, we have largely seen Democratic officials band together after primaries when a progressive or DSA candidate won. In Michigan, for instance, nearly all of the Democrats quickly endorsed Abdul El-Sayed. Most voters are not strongly ideological. When I’ve talked to political scientists and pollsters, they often will note that these debates over internal party labelling are high level, and that most voters don’t really care if a Democrat is a progressive, DSA, moderate in a general election. Where we’ve seen the most detraction from a sense of moderates embracing the left is from the pundit and consultant class, and I don’t know if that’s all that influential on voter behavior – though it certainly takes up a lot of media airtime.

blocks.caption: Democratic socialist Abdul El-Sayed was quickly endorsed by Democrats after his primary win. Photograph: Rebecca Cook/Reuters

blocks.text: What should the primary focus be for Democrats if they win?

KafkasDog asks: Trumpism has substantially distressed your democracy. If the Dems are in control of the House and Senate after November should their primary focus be on addressing and repairing the damage or bringing Trumpism to heel?

double quotation markDavid: It has to be both. Democrats should try to stop the rot, blocking funding for ICE and the Iran war, launching investigations into corruption (including Trump’s makeover of Washington), trying to protect the independence of the justice department and so on. We may see another debate over to impeach or to not impeach. But they also need to offer a positive agenda as an antidote to Trumpism. It’s not enough to say “We’re not Trump” or to promise “We’ll turn back the clock to 2015”.
Can being too united be a bad thing?

Lauramax100 asks: Could being too united be a bad thing? It was a real turn-off when party elders tried so hard to interfere in the NYC mayoral election even after primary voters made their choice. Could celebrating a broad coalition and letting local people choose be a better approach? The Republicans weren’t totally united pre-Trump, and arguably his attempt to have an iron grip on all GOP politicians may be one part of that party’s undoing.

double quotation markJoseph: Unity can easily tip into groupthink, and the reluctance of leaders like Schumer and Jeffries to back Mamdani after he clearly (resoundingly?) won the primary looked to many like exactly that … the elite and old guard second-guessing where the voters have moved, which is why even allies like AOC called it a bad look. Trump’s “iron grip” model has won elections, but I’d argue it’s brittle: it depends on near-total deference to one man, punishes dissent that might otherwise catch mistakes early, and leaves the party with little to correct course once he’s gone. The Democrats’ instinct to litigate every nominee’s ideological purity risks the opposite type of failure. It’s a party so busy relitigating primaries that it struggles to actually fight the other side. They must come to terms with what the voters are not asking for, but now demanding of their elected officials.

double quotation markDavid: I agree with Joseph that the Trump cult is brittle: like an authoritarian regime, investing so much in one leader means a lack of flexibility and diversity of thought. And, like an authoritarian regime, Republicans will now have to wrestle with the succession question of who comes next. Democrats holding feisty debates of ideas is a healthier way to go. But as we’ve seen, especially in the social media era, that can easily become corrosive and turn into a circular firing squad. Some have observed that Democratic moderates are more venomous towards progressives than they are towards Republicans! They have to get the balance right and unite around their nominee in 2028.

blocks.caption: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries has been slow to embrace winning members of the progressive left   Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/AP

blocks.text: What are the races to watch to understand the state of the Democrats?

nycreader2 asks: Abdul El-Sayed has become a major symbol of the debate over the party’s direction. Are there other races or candidates we should be watching if we want to understand where Democrats are heading?

double quotation markRachel Leingang: There are so many interesting races this year – and I don’t think there will be one clean narrative about who wins. El-Sayed’s race remains one of the most interesting, though Democrats (and a couple independents) in typically redder places could win running economic populist campaigns that largely avoid cultural issues, and there will likely be more progressives in Congress based on who won the primaries. I’m based in the Midwest, so I’m paying close attention to: – David Crowley vs Tom Tiffany in the Wisconsin governor’s race – Rebecca Cooke’s third attempt to unseat Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s third congressional district – Basically every federal and statewide race in Iowa: Rob Sand for governor, Josh Turek for Senate, three of the four congressional races – Dan Osborn’s run as an independent for US Senate in Nebraska, as well as a couple congressional campaigns there – Adam Hamilton, a Democratic pastor, is making a case he could win in Kansas – Sherrod Brown’s attempt to return to the US Senate in Ohio, along with a few congressional races there that could flip seats – In Michigan, Will Lawrence’s progressive campaign in a split district

blocks.caption: Rebecca Cooke is running for the third time to unseat Derrick Van Orden Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/AP

blocks.text: double quotation markShrai Popat: Just to piggyback off Rachel here, a few that I’ve been covering and fascinated by across the country: – Troy Jackson in Maine. He’s the replacement Democratic nominee after the truly wild primary race blew up when Graham Platner was accused of sexual assault (which he denies) and ended his campaign. Jackson, who is a logger and former state lawmaker, is trying to unseat Susan Collins – a moderate Republican who is hoping to secure a sixth term in office. – Chris Pappas in New Hampshire. He’s a moderate congressman who has kept his once purple district blue. He’s hoping to keep the open Senate seat in Democratic control, but facing a tough contest against John E Sununu – a former senator from a political dynasty who has been comfortable criticizing Trump in the past (even though he bagged the president’s endorsement this cycle). Notably, Pappas beat his progressive challenger in the primary. New Hampshire really is emblematic of what a purple state looks like. Fully Democratic congressional delegation but Republican control of the legislature. Harris won in 2024, but the state still elected a GOP governor. What’s interesting to me in both of these New England Senate races is how Trump’s support could easily be an albatross for both of these Republicans as opposed to an asset. They’ll have to navigate unpopular opinions about the administration among moderates/swing voters, but also satisfy the Maga base. Another race that continues to be a prime example of picking a Democratic nominee with huge momentum is the Texas Senate race. Here, James Talarico, a polished state lawmaker, is facing a Trump loyalist – Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general. Talarico has touted his religious beliefs, and walked back some of his more socially progressive comments. He’s also praised the incumbent senator John Cornyn, who lost the GOP primary to Paxton this year.
Will the Democrats consolidate the way Republicans did around Trump?

NorthLondonIsRed asks: Since Zohran Mamdani’s election as NYC Mayor some Democratic leaders (Schumer, Jeffries) have kept their distance from him and the DSA, while others (Hochul, Harris, AOC, Sanders) have pushed for unity. As the party’s left wing gains national visibility ahead of the 2026 midterms will Democrats consolidate the way the GOP did under Trump — or will the centrist/progressive divide deepen into a functional three-party split?

double quotation markDavid Smith says: I think they’ll be fine before the midterms. They will have progressives running in some districts and moderates in others, with anti-Trump sentiment as the glue holding them together. One exception might be Michigan, where many Democrats have got on board with progressive Abdul El-Sayed but some have not. After the midterms, however, there is potential for a split. If El-Sayed loses, there will be lots of finger pointing and claims that a progressive can’t win in 2028. But if El-Sayed and democratic socialists do well, it could be game on for Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 2028.

double quotation markAlice Speri: I don’t think this is going to be as much of an issue in the midterms. I think even Democrats who are unhappy about the DSA wins will prioritize defeating Republicans. I do think these tensions will be dominating the presidential primaries though and many are already gearing up for that. Third Way, a centrist Democratic group, announced a $15m effort to go to “war” against DSA. I don’t think that whatever unity Democrats manage to find in November will last.

blocks.caption: Zohran Mamdani at his victory party last year. Will  Democrats consolidate the way Republicans did around Trump? Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian

blocks.text: Welcome to the Conversation
We’re less than two months from the midterm elections that could have an outsized impact on the future of the United States.
With the primaries wrapped, our reporting team is fanned out across the country to tell the stories behind the horse race, from Washington to the Midwest and along the West Coast.

One of the key questions is, with the Democrats poised to take the House and perhaps even the Senate, what the rise of the party’s progressive left means for the broader Democrat coalition. How will candidates such as Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed co-exist with the party’s more established centrists – and will the growing influence of democratic socialists push the party in a new direction?

Political breaking news correspondent Joseph Gedeon, Midwest political correspondent, Rachel Leingang, US politics live blogger Shrai Popat; Washington bureau chief David Smith and reporter, Alice Speri are here live answering your questions.
Sign up or sign in to join the discussion.

articles.title: Pia Cayetano: 'I fear for my right to speak'
articles.summary: Senator Pia Cayetano on Wednesday said she was feeling fear and pressure as more members of the minority bloc face cases amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 12:00am
Senator Pia Cayetano on Wednesday said she was feeling fear and pressure as more members of the minority bloc face cases amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

During a session where senator-judges heard insights from four retired Supreme justices on the voting threshold for conviction, Cayetano said she had observed that several senators had been unable to attend the hearings.

Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, while Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the Duterte administration’s war on drugs.
Senator Loren Legarda has not attended the trial for several weeks as she remains abroad on extended medical leave.

“I went to Singapore to support a national team, and then I have to hear the NBI director making statements that make it appear that I’m a common fugitive, na na-monitor niya kung nasaan ako at meron siyang information kung anong araw ako babalik. Am I a fugitive? Bakit may ganito? (That he monitored where I was and had information on when I would return. Am I a fugitive? Why is it like this?)” Cayetano said.

“I will tell you all now, am I pressured? I am. I am. I fear for my liberty. Even in the Senate, we have a colleague, na walang katapusang tantanan kami (Even in the Senate, we have a colleague who just won’t stop going after us.). I fear for my right to speak,” she added.

“So, what will happen now? Do I excuse myself? Pero kung hindi gagalawin 'yang number na iyan eh di nakakapagsalita tayo rito nang maayos (But if that number is not changed, then we can speak freely here),” she said, apparently referring to Presiding Officer Francis Escudero’s ruling that under the 1987 Constitution conviction requires at least 16 affirmative votes, or two-thirds of all members of the Senate.
Senator Pia Cayetano and her brother, Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, traveled to Singapore on September 9 and returned to the Philippines on September 12.
According to the Bureau of Immigration, there was no hold departure order or derogatory record that would have prevented the Cayetanos from traveling abroad. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: DepEd taps 170 leaders to boost SHS graduates’ employability
articles.summary: The Department of Education has tapped the assistance of more than 170 leaders across government, industry and strategic economic sectors in implementing the work immersion program under the…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Education Secretary Sonny Angara.
DepEd Facebook page

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) has tapped the assistance of more than 170 leaders across government, industry and strategic economic sectors in implementing the work immersion program under the Strengthened Senior High School (SHS) curriculum to improve the employability of graduates.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara said closing the gap between schools and industry requires urgent, ground-level execution.

The DepEd is streamlining the senior high school framework from four tracks to two: Academic and Technical-Professional (TechPro), giving learners greater subject flexibility while embedding intensive, industry-guided work immersion options.
For TechPro learners, the enhanced work immersion program will feature structured joint training plans, hands-on mentoring and industry assessments tied directly to national skills certifications.

Industry leaders underscored the need to embed strict workplace safety standards, essential soft skills and ethical values into early career training to help learners succeed in high-demand environments.
Partner associations expressed strong support for structured immersion models, with initial industry commitments already pledging around 31,000 work immersion slots.
This represents more than 60 percent of DepEd’s 50,000-slot target across over 1,100 distinct job roles.

“We are refining our curriculum and expanding our Enhanced Work Immersion Program because our learners deserve real pathways to quality jobs, entrepreneurship and higher learning. We cannot build a future-ready economy with yesterday’s skills framework,” Angara said.

articles.title: Ferry fire death toll hits 77
articles.summary: One of the survivors of the MV June Aster fire has died in a hospital in Palawan, the Philippine Coast Guard said yesterday.

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) recovered 30 bodies from MV June Aster, which were brought to the Port of Borac, on September 12, 2026 afternoon following the ferry fire off Coron, Palawan on September 9, 2026.
MANILA, Philippines — One of the survivors of the MV June Aster fire has died in a hospital in Palawan, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said yesterday.
Fatalities are now at 77, with 43 survivors and 12 missing.
The June Aster crewman died on Tuesday at the Culion Sanitarium General Hospital, PCG spokesperson Noemie Cayabyab told radio dzBB.
Roel Sarmiento, the ship’s captain, said he tried to warn people about the fire, but the vessel’s public address system failed after June Aster lost its power.
In a testimony, Sarmiento recalled assisting passengers and feeling dazed upon returning to land.
“Due to so much trauma, I just walked down a road until I arrived wherever,” he said.
Cayabyab said the PCG will conduct maritime safety and crime investigations.
June Aster caught fire on Sept. 9 following an explosion in the cargo hold.
Atienza Interisland Ferries owns the ship.

articles.title: 14 Pinoys ‘recruited’ by Russia for Ukraine war
articles.summary: Fourteen Filipinos were reportedly recruited in Russia and lured into combat roles for its war against Ukraine, a security expert said yesterday.

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am

A Ukrainian serviceman is seen in the window of a damaged residential building at Koshytsa Street, a suburb of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, where a military shell allegedly hit, on February 25, 2022. Russian forces reached the outskirts of Kyiv on Friday as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the invading troops were targeting civilians and explosions could be heard in the besieged capital. Pre-dawn blasts in Kyiv set off a second day of violence after Russian President Vladimir Putin defied Western warnings to unleash a full-scale ground invasion and air assault on Thursday that quickly claimed dozens of lives and displaced at least 100,000 people.
AFP / Daniel Leal
MANILA, Philippines — Fourteen Filipinos were reportedly recruited in Russia and lured into combat roles for its war against Ukraine, a security expert said yesterday.
Of the 14 Filipinos allegedly fighting for Moscow, Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group, said one was killed and another is a prisoner of war.
“So far, the alleged count of Filipinos is 14,” Mustaffa said in a European Union- organized online discussion on Russia’s recruitment of nationals from Asia for its war in Ukraine.

Mustaffa, also the founder of Chasseur Group, a security consultancy based in Kuala Lumpur and a senior fellow at Verve Research, an independent think tank focused on Southeast Asian security and foreign policy, wrote the report “Southeast Asia’s Mercenary Pipeline.”
She said the Filipinos were not aware they were recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine war.
In January, a Filipino fighting alongside Russian forces was killed in Ukraine. He was named by Ukraine’s intelligence services as among those killed in the Donetsk region.

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Marcos administration has released roughly 94.1 percent of the P6.793-trillion national budget as of end-August, a slightly slower pace than the previous year’s, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said.
Data from the Status of Allotment Releases report showed that the DBM released P6.39 trillion in the first eight months of the year, representing 94.1 percent of the total allocation.
This leaves about P401.38 billion still to be released in the remaining four months.
The releases are behind the 95.5 percent allotment release rate posted in the same period under the 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA).
Of the total released under the 2026 GAA, P3.47 trillion went to government departments, with a release rate of 94.5 percent of the adjusted P3.67-trillion programmed budget.

Among major agencies that had relatively lower release rates of their programs are the Department of Agriculture (DA) and Department of Tourism (DOT), which received below 90 percent of their program as of end-August.
The DA had only 68.8 percent of its P163.26-billion budget, slower than the 96.7 percent release rate posted a year ago.
Meanwhile, the DOT had P4.05 billion, or 87.4 percent, of its P4.64-billion adjusted program released.
The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) received 99.5 percent of its P530.12-billion budget as of end-August.
The Department of Education, which has the highest allocation in the national budget, received 92.5 percent of its record-high P961.14-billion budget, below last year’s 95.9-percent pace.
In terms of special purpose funds, the government has already released P518.52 billion, which is 72.1 percent of the adjusted P719.07-billion budget.
Automatic appropriations are at 89.9 percent or P2.16 trillion of the P2.4-trillion aggregate funding.
On the other hand, P120.11 billion was released for unprogrammed appropriations, particularly to support foreign-assisted projects.

Unprogrammed appropriations provide standby authority to incur additional agency obligations for priority programs or projects when revenue collection exceeds targets or when additional grants or foreign funds are generated.

The bulk of the unprogrammed appropriations, worth P80.15 billion, went to the Department of Transportation, P25.55 billion to DPWH, P13.88 billion to the Department of Social Welfare and Development, P511.03 million to Philippine Competition Commission and P23.79 million to the Department of Health.
PhilHealth budget

The government is proposing P74.45 billion for the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) in 2027, including P19 billion for improvements to benefit packages and other priority health interventions, according to the DBM.

The P19-billion funding is intended to support improvements in health benefits covering priority concerns such as mental health and severe malnutrition, as well as assistance involving hospitals operated by local government units (LGUs).

It will also cover the national government’s premium subsidies for qualified beneficiaries. About 11.09 million beneficiaries are targeted to receive the subsidies in 2027, up from around 10.65 million in 2026.
The proposed funding comes as the government implements measures intended to reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenses for hospitalization.

In September, the DBM approved P10.377 billion for the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing (ZBB) program, including P9.377 billion for DOH hospitals nationwide and P1 billion for six pilot LGU hospitals in Benguet, Batangas, Laguna, Quezon, Aklan and Sarangani.
The DBM also released an additional P800 million to the Philippine General Hospital, specifically for ZBB.
DBM acting Secretary Kim Robert de Leon said government spending on health should result in direct assistance to patients.
“Every peso we release for health must ultimately reach the patient,” De Leon said in August.
He reiterated the point following the approval of the P10.377-billion ZBB funding.

“No Filipino should have to choose between obtaining the medical care they need and protecting their family from a hospital bill they cannot afford. This P10.377-billion release is intended to ensure that when our people become ill, the government is there to help shoulder the financial burden,” De Leon said.

The proposed PhilHealth allocation is part of the P353.8-billion health sector budget proposed for 2027. It also includes P107.29 billion for the operations of 72 DOH regional hospitals and other health facilities, P25.39 billion for the National Health Workforce Support System and P3.75 billion for the Cancer Assistance Fund.

PhilHealth received a total of P129.8 billion in government funding in 2026, following an initial P53.13-billion subsidy that was supplemented by P60 billion in funding recovery support and an additional P16.52 billion from the bicameral conference committee. – Christine Boton

articles.title: Escudero hits prosecutors for violating sub judice rule
articles.summary: Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero yesterday issued show-cause orders against members of the House prosecution panel amid alleged violation of the sub judice ruling in the ongoing impeachment…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Presiding officer Chiz Escudero made a lighthearted comment about private prosecutor Atty. Mae Divinagracia’s hoarse voice during the 18th day of the impeachment trial on August 25, 2026.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero yesterday issued show-cause orders against members of the House prosecution panel amid alleged violation of the sub judice ruling in the ongoing impeachment trial against Vice President Sara Duterte.
Escudero did not disclose the names of the members of the prosecution team who were included in the show cause orders.

Escudero has vowed the sub judice rule will be strictly enforced in Duterte’s impeachment trial as he has warned of public reprimand and admonition on the first offense and a P30,000 fine on the second.
He warned the prosecution – both the public and private panels – and the defense team that they could face contempt of court if they violated the sub judice rule.
Baste subpoenaed
Meanwhile, Escudero approved the issuance of a subpoena for Duterte’s brother, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte.

“In regard to Mayor Sebastian Duterte… let the subpoena be issued only for Sept. 23. However, on Sept. 22, depending on where we are with respect to the three witnesses, we shall announce if we will be withdrawing that subpoena and simply issue a new one for the following week or the week thereafter. So as not to waste their time, given that they are all officials performing duties in connection with their functions,” Escudero said.
Defense spokesman Michael Poa said that it is the prerogative of the prosecution to request a subpoena for the mayor.

articles.title: Fluid vote threshold open to abuse – Azcuna
articles.summary: A changeable vote threshold can be easily manipulated by ruling political factions, retired Supreme Court associate justice Adolfo Azcuna warned yesterday, as he defended maintaining the required…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Retired Supreme Court associate justice and former member of the Constitutional Commission Adolfo Azcuna.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — A changeable vote threshold can be easily manipulated by ruling political factions, retired Supreme Court associate justice Adolfo Azcuna warned yesterday, as he defended maintaining the required votes needed to convict an impeachable official at two-thirds of all 24 senators.

Responding to questions submitted by Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense counsel and read to the court by presiding officer Francis Escudero, the 1987 Constitution framer explained that basing the two-thirds threshold solely on actual attendance invites dangerous abuse.
“There is no guarantee. That’s the danger seen by the drafters of our Constitution. That’s why they made as basis or denominator the total membership of the Senate and Congress,” Azcuna said.
Asked if lowering the threshold could encourage a ruling administration to jail opposing lawmakers or deny them bail to skew numbers, Azcuna answered in the affirmative.

“There’s the danger of it getting abused by the president, not only the president, but even by members of the Senate, whoever controls the power of who can attend, who can prevent fellow members from attending… if you make the threshold dependent on actual attendance,” Azcuna said.

Retired chief justice Reynato Puno warned that any deliberate plot by a political faction to engineer absences and alter the voting base would render the trial unconstitutional. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Panganiban to Risa: You’re single... I’m single

Sen. Risa Hontiveros.

MANILA, Philippines — Retired chief justice Artemio Panganiban drew some uncomfortable laughter in the plenary yesterday after teasing Sen. Risa Hontiveros.
At Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Hontiveros asked for Panganiban’s thoughts on her questions to the other retired justices.
“Can I also reply in our private conversation?” the widower said.
Confusing Hontiveros with what he meant, Panganiban quipped: “Dalaga naman po kayo (You are single).”
Going along with the joke, presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero asked Hontiveros: “Can you confirm?”
“Binata rin ako (I am also single),” Panganiban told Hontiveros, a widow.

articles.title: House adopts Senate bill on BSKE
articles.summary: In a move to hasten the process, the House of Representatives has decided to adopt the approved measure of the Senate providing five-year terms for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials as the…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am

“We have been informed that the committee on local government, sponsor of House Bill 10971 as well as authors thereof, are in concurrence with the provisions of Senate Bill 2387,” Sorsogon Rep. Bernadette Escudero said.
STAR / Ernie Penaredondo

MANILA, Philippines — In a move to hasten the process, the House of Representatives has decided to adopt the approved measure of the Senate providing five-year terms for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials as the BSK elections on Nov. 2 draw near.
“In accordance with our rules, I move to adopt SB 2387 as an amendment to HB 10971,” she declared during yesterday’s plenary session.
The Senate and House measures seek to postpone the Nov. 2 BSKE this year and move this to the second Monday of November 2028, or a few months after the May 2028 presidential elections.

The House’s decision does away with the convening of the bicameral conference committee where senators and congressmen will still have to discuss and reconcile conflicting versions of their respective bills. Through this, HB 10971 will then be harmonized with SB 2387.
Senators have set a two-term limit for village officials and a single-term for youth officials.

The same measure also provided that beneficiaries of the two-year extension will be considered to have served one full five-year term, while those on their last term will be prohibited from seeking another term for the same position.

articles.title: Romualdez pleads not guilty in P7.4 billion plunder case
articles.summary: Leyte representative and former speaker Martin Romualdez has pleaded not guilty to plunder charges over his alleged P7.4-billion kickbacks from flood control projects.

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Leyte representative and former speaker Martin Romualdez has pleaded not guilty to plunder charges over his alleged P7.4-billion kickbacks from flood control projects.
Romualdez, in a wheelchair, entered his plea yesterday at the New Quezon City Jail after the Sandiganbayan Third Division allowed his arraignment via video conferencing.
The anti-graft court, however, denied for lack of merit his request for waiving of the reading of the formal charges against him.
It also denied his plea to be transferred to a tertiary hospital in Quezon City, emphasizing that the lawmaker is well enough to stay at the New Quezon City Jail.

Third Division chairman Associate Justice Karl Miranda cited the findings of the Philippine General Hospital, which stated that Romualdez is clinically stable and does not require further hospital confinement.

“The mere invocation of ill health is not sufficient for an accused’s continued confinement in a hospital,” Miranda said. “There are many more PDLs (persons deprived of liberty) that have worse medical conditions compared to congressman Romualdez.”
With Romualdez during his arraignment was lawyer Jose Roy III.
Since the lawmaker pleaded not guilty, the case was automatically submitted for trial. The court has set pre-marking of evidence on Sept. 18, 21, 22, 23 and 24.
Martin to seek bail
Romualdez’s camp said he would file a petition for bail.
The anti-graft court gave Romualdez 10 days to explain why he should not be preventively suspended while on trial for plunder.
Another Romualdez lawyer, Ade Fajardo, said they requested for video conferencing to avoid “contracting an emergency situation” as the lawmaker’s condition is still fragile.

He also said they had requested for a waiver of the reading of the formal charges because Romualdez – himself a lawyer – is aware of the charges against him. Moreover, Fajardo said, the reading of charges was “additional stress” to Romualdez.
“He is maintaining his innocence and we’re in pre-trial proceedings wherein we laid down the evidence, and we have to have all these marked for orderly trial proceedings,” he said.

“If the evidence is strong, the Sandiganbayan can deny the petition for bail. That’s why we are proceeding to the petition for bail so that the prosecution can finally present to the court what their evidence is,” Fajardo said.
He said they would also discuss requesting the court’s permission to allow Romualdez not to physically appear at his trial.
Romualdez, tagged as the “central figure” by the Office of the Ombudsman in the multibillion-peso flood control kickback scheme, was charged with plunder on Sept. 7.
When an arrest warrant was issued, the lawmaker was already confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center for cardiovascular event and a supposed panic attack.

Authorities then served the warrant and conducted booking procedures in the hospital. They released photos of Romualdez, showing him lying in a hospital bed, with a detainee shirt draped over his hospital gown.
Romualdez’s co-accused in the plunder charges are former lawmaker and fugitive Zaldy Co and private individuals Joselyn Serenio and Felicito Guevarra.

His detention at the infirmary ward of the New Quezon City Jail was not a form of special treatment, as it was made upon the recommendations of doctors of the PGH where the legislator stayed over the weekend, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla emphasized.
“While you might think that the way he was treated was over and above – well just check the commitment orders and recommendation from PGH,” Remulla said.
Wait-and-see

But the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte said it is not yet convinced of the sincerity of the administration in holding corrupt officials accountable despite the filing of plunder case against Romualdez.

“We can’t make a judgment early because we haven’t seen the specific accusations against Martin Romualdez and the specific evidence. Isn’t it easy to file a case? They’ve already filed a lot with the VP, I hope there is no basis,” Duterte’s spokesman and lawyer Paolo Panelo said in a chance interview.
“Whether the correct basis was used to file this complaint against Martin Romualdez, if our government is really serious, let’s wait and see,” Panelo said. – Emmanuel Tupas, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Shock and anger in Kosovo as former president convicted
articles.summary: The conviction in The Hague of former President Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders has caused consternation in Kosovo — both among political leaders and on the streets. DW…

image.caption: A protester waves an Albanian flag outside the headquarters of the European Union Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo (EULEX) after former President Hashim Thaci was found guilty of war crimes by the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The HagueImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: The announcement of the verdict was greeted with shock and profound disappointment in Pristina.

Thousands of citizens had gathered in the main square of Kosovo's capital, many waving flags of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), to follow the announcement live on large screens. Similar gatherings took place across the country in Kosovo's main cities.

When it became clear that the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague had found former President Hashim Thaci, and former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi guilty of war crimes, the crowd fell silent.
The initial silence was then followed by calls for justice and chants of support for the four men.

Groups of citizens began trying to demolish sections of the perimeter wall surrounding EULEX, the EU Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo, which was deployed in Kosovo after the country's declaration of independence from neighboring Serbia in 2008 and continues to operate to this day.

blocks.caption: Thousands of people gathered in Pristina to watch a livestream of the verdict in the war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The HagueImage: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

blocks.text: Large numbers of Kosovo police officers and special units intervened to prevent further damage and incidents.
Political leaders in Kosovo respond
But it wasn't just the people on the streets who were disappointed; the country's political leaders were quick to respond to the news from The Hague.

Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca, who was present in the courtroom in The Hague when the verdict was announced, said that "the conviction of the former KLA leaders is a terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war," describing it as "a major blow to the state and to the domestic narrative."
"Kosovo experienced the war itself. We know what the KLA war was about and we know that there was no criminal mechanism to harm any population. It is a sad, unjust and undeserved decision," he said.
Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti labelled the verdict an "unacceptable injustice."
"The conviction and such a severe sentence for four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army is an unacceptable injustice, a great and harmful punishment," he said on Wednesday.

The Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), a party founded immediately after the war by Hashim Thaci and several other former KLA leaders, described the guilty verdict as an "unjust and unacceptable judgment," stressing that "the battle for justice continues until the very end."

"In The Hague, the right of our people, who fought for freedom, survival and liberation from the Serbian state regime that killed, expelled and terrorized Kosovo Albanians, was dealt a severe blow. For us, this judgment represents a major injustice because it is based on allegations and material that we consider fabricated and which, over the years, have been promoted by the Serbian state apparatus and propaganda in an effort to criminalize the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army," the PDK said in a statement.

The response from Kosovo's acting president, Albulena Haxhiu, was similar. She described the convictions of the four men as "a severe blow to their families, deeply shocking news for the Republic of Kosovo and a grave moment for the Albanian nation wherever it lives."

"On a day like this, the weight of this decision cannot be separated from the history from which we have emerged," Haxhiu wrote in her statement. "Kosovo experienced first-hand the violence of a state apparatus that killed civilians, committed massacres, expelled hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes and left behind thousands of people killed or missing. This experience is an indelible part of the memory of Kosovo and the Albanian nation."
Charges of crimes against humanity dismissed

More than three years after the start of the trial and nearly six years after the four men were charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1998–99 Kosovo War, the panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague handed down guilty verdicts against former KLA leaders Hashim Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Hashim Thaci listen to the announcement of the verdict against the former president and three other former KLA leaders Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

blocks.text: While the three-judge panel dismissed the charges of crimes against humanity, the four men were convicted of war crimes against civilians and political opponents who did not support the KLA during the war.

Hashim Thaci, who was indicted while serving as president of Kosovo, was sentenced to 25 years in prison. Jakup Krasniqi, who served as a KLA spokesman and later as speaker of Kosovo's parliament on several occasions, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison. Kadri Veseli, who headed the KLA intelligence service during the war, was sentenced to 18 years in prison, and Rexhep Selimi, who served as chief inspector of the KLA military police, was sentenced to 13 years in prison.
Defense lawyers for the men said they would appeal the verdict.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which was set up by the Kosovo Assembly (parliament) in 2015, is staffed by international judges and based in The Hague. It deals exclusively with cases relating to allegations of crimes committed by members of the KLA during the Kosovo War.
Before returning to join Kosovo's struggle for independence in 1998, Hashim Thaci had been a student in Switzerland.

As a political leader of the former KLA, he received support from Western leaders, who invited him to participate in the 1999 peace talks in Rambouillet, France. At the time, Thaci was seen in Kosovo as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.

Around 13,000 civilians — most of them Kosovo Albanians — were killed and around one million people were displaced during the war, which saw Kosovo, at the time a Serbian province, fighting for independence from Serbia.

blocks.caption: Protesters also gathered outside the building that houses the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague after the verdict was announcedImage: Omar Havana/REUTERS

blocks.text: Following NATO's intervention against Serbian forces and their withdrawal from Kosovo, Thaci founded his own political party and came to power, first as Kosovo's prime minister and later as president.

In 2008, Kosovo declared independence from Serbia, a move rejected and still not recognized by authorities in Belgrade, Moscow and Beijing. Kosovo's statehood is, however, recognized by over 100 countries.
Relations between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite more than 15 years of negotiations between the two countries, mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.
Thaci, who like the other three men, denied the charges against him, resigned as president of Kosovo in 2020 to face the charges and defend himself in The Hague.

articles.title: Obama family dog Sunny dies: ‘a force of nature’
articles.summary:
Sunny, who joined the Obama family at the White House in 2013, was the second Obama dog after Bo, who died in 2021

Sunny Obama, the Obama family’s second beloved Portuguese Water Dog, died…

blocks.text: Sunny Obama, the Obama family’s second beloved Portuguese Water Dog, died on Tuesday, Barack Obama announced on Wednesday morning.
“Yesterday, we lost a cherished member of our family,” the former president wrote on social media, attaching a photo of the 14-year-old dog whom he called “a force of nature”.
Sunny joined the Obama family at the White House in 2013 during Obama’s second term. She was the second Obama dog after Bo, who died in 2021.

Unlike Bo, Sunny was known for her energetic disposition, occasionally making headlines for her rowdiness – like in 2013 when she knocked over a toddler during a White House holiday party or in 2017 when Sunny allegedly bit a visitor on the face.
“She loved the girls, even if they were pestering her when she was napping. She loved our team, and would often follow them around, helping them on the job,” Obama said.

Sunny was born in June 2012 in Michigan but joined the Obamas at the White House in August 2013. She was obtained from a breeder and, upon announcing her arrival, the family made a donation to the Washington Humane Society.
The family chose to name her Sunny to “fit her cheerful personality”.
“We will miss her terribly, and imagine she’s with her big brother now, making sure he’s okay,” Obama wrote.

articles.title: Annie Dillard, Pulitzer prize-winning author of nonfiction and nature essays, dies aged 81
articles.summary:
Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, published when Dillard was 28, skyrocketed her to become one of the most prominent nonfiction writers of her generation

Annie Dillard, author of the Pulitzer…

blocks.text: Annie Dillard, author of the Pulitzer prize-winning book Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, died aged 81 at her home in South Wellfleet, Massachusetts on Tuesday.
Maggie Nelson, Dillard’s literary editor, confirmed her death to the New York Times.

Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, a nonfiction narrative Dillard wrote about the natural world surrounding her mountainous Virginia home, was published in 1974 when the young writer was just 28. The book was an instant critical and financial success, skyrocketing Dillard to becoming one of the most prominent nonfiction writers of her generation.
Tinker Creek won the 1975 Pulitzer Prize for general nonfiction, and in 1998 it was included in Modern Library’s list of 100 best nonfiction books.

Initially overwhelmed by her sudden fame and countless requests for interviews, the introspective Dillard retreated to Washington state and started splitting her time between the city of Bellingham and the islands Waldron and Lummi.

Over the years, Dillard went on to publish poetry, essays, journalism, meditations on religion, theory of literature, two novels and a bestselling autobiography. Her eerie essay, 1982’s Total Eclipse, about her experience witnessing a solar eclipse three years earlier, was chosen by Joyce Carol Oates as among the 20th century’s 100 best essays.
Dillard published her autobiography An American Childhood in 1987, which covered her years growing up during the 1950s and 1960s in the Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania area.
In 1992, she published her debut novel, The Living, a piece of historical fiction exploring the lives of European settlers and a group of Lummi natives in late 19th century Washington.

Dillard was well known throughout her career for her tremendous range as a writer. Her acute ability to capture the astonishment that humans feel in the face of wilderness and the plurality of the world left readers astonished, and her choice to live life surrounded by the wonders of nature was reflected directly in her craft.

Her work was often compared to Henry David Thoreau, the naturalist about whom she wrote her master’s thesis. Despite the association, Dillard rejected the pigeonhole label of “nature writer”, instead considering herself a theologian pondering the mystery of God and the duality of reality.

In the 1989 collection of short essays, titled The Writing Life, she wrote “how we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives”. Dillard spent her days outdoors taking notes and contemplating everything.

Dillard was married three times, most recently to historical biographer Robert D Richardson, whom she was married to for 32 years until his death in 2020. She had one daughter, Cody Rose, born in 1984 in Connecticut.

articles.title: Former French culture minister goes on trial on corruption charges
articles.summary: Rachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliament

blocks.text: Rachida Dati, a former French culture minister, has gone on trial in Paris on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan carmaking group.

Dati, 60, is accused of illegal lobbying when she accepted €900,000 (£770,000) in lawyer’s fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan while she was a member of the European parliament. The court will have to decide what the money was for.

Dati’s legal team denied all corruption allegations, saying she worked “exclusively” as a lawyer for the Renault-Nissan subsidiary. French prosecutors argue that she was instead paid to lobby for the carmaking group, an activity that is banned for members of the European parliament. Prosecutors said there was a lack of evidence to show Dati had carried out legal work.
Dati was placed under investigation in 2019 on suspicion of illegally lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013, when she was an MEP.

Dati is on trial with Carlos Ghosn, the disgraced former Renault-Nissan chief, who will be tried in absentia. Ghosn, 72, was detained in Japan in November 2018 amid allegations of financial misconduct in a separate case involving a plot to falsify records about his personal pay in order to enrich himself. He dodged trial in Japan after escaping to Lebanon in an audio equipment case. He has denied all wrongdoing in the Japan case as well as in the Dati case.

French prosecutors argue that a legal services contract signed in 2009 between Dati and Ghosn, in which Dati was paid an annual fee of €300,000, was used to disguise lobbying work. Investigators obtained the contract in 2019 during a search of Renault’s headquarters after Ghosn’s arrest in Japan.

Dati, 60, who is the district mayor of the 7th arrondissement in Paris, is one of the most prominent figures on the French right. She was the first woman of north African and Muslim heritage to hold a major French government post when she was appointed justice minister by the rightwing president Nicolas Sarkozy. She returned to government under Emmanuel Macron, as culture minister.

Dati redefined political celebrity in France, and has said growing up as the second of 11 children on a low-income housing estate on the outskirts of Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy gave her a greater understanding of the French electorate. She ran for mayor of Paris earlier this year, but lost to the Socialist Emmanuel Grégoire.
If convicted, Dati faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to €450,000. She could also face a five-year ban on holding public office.
Dati’s lawyers said: “Unfounded allegations of influence peddling in the European parliament stem from an artificial intellectual construct devised by the prosecution.”
after newsletter promotion

In a separate investigation, Dati has been accused of accepting nearly €300,000 in undeclared payments from the energy group GDF Suez, also while an MEP. Prosecutors said last year they were looking into reports Dati failed to declare jewellery and watches worth €420,000 upon taking ministerial office.
She has denied any wrongdoing in all cases.

articles.title: Sweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening?
articles.summary: Even as the ‘extremist’ AfD seeks further election gains in Germany, Europe’s leaders can learn from Sweden’s dangerous embrace with far-right ideology

blocks.text: Europe’s focus turned nervously to Sweden on Sunday, after an explosive election in Germany just a week earlier placed a far-right party, officially classed as “extremist”, on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the Nazi era. A party with neo-Nazi roots has been pulling the government’s strings in Sweden for the last four years – would the country’s general election put the far right formally in government? Or would enough Swedes opt for a gear change, having seen the Sweden Democrats’ hardline (some would say poisonous) agenda in action?

Votes were still being counted on Wednesday but it was immediately clear that the far-right Sweden Democrats had suffered a setback; their first loss of support among voters since it entered parliament for the first time 16 years ago. The party slipped from being the country’s second biggest party to its third.

The centre-left Social Democrats appear poised for a return to power, although it could take months for their leader, Magdalena Andersson, to form a coalition. Strong results for the left and green parties gave her left bloc a wafer-thin, three-seat majority.

Is the far right’s regression, however modest, a turning point? Have Swedes reached the limits of a taboo-busting experiment with populist, nationalist rightwing prescriptions? And is there a message for mainstream leaders across Europe, many of whom seem fatalistic about a continental far-right surge? France goes to the polls in April while governments in Italy, Spain and Poland, all face their electorates later next year.

The Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde says elections in one country are a poor guide to what will happen in another. Specific local factors in Sweden, including a scandal, may have dented the far right’s support. For Mudde, the scale of the AfD’s win in Saxony Anhalt, however, was “a black day for Europe” – and with far-right ideas gaining ground across the continent, he warned mainstream politicians that “today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power”.

This is where Sweden offers a cautionary tale. Its political establishment had “fully normalised” the far-right party, Mudde said. “Its nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.”
But the decline in the far right’s support, for now, he thinks, “at the very least creates space for mainstream parties to focus on issues other than immigration”.

Ann-Cathrine Jungar, a professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, is very sure that the Sweden Democrats are not on the way out. Electoral rankings go up and down, she said, and the party’s influence will endure. More important now is how the mainstream parties respond.

“We focus a lot on the extreme and radical right parties, but the key to their influence is what the other parties do. Why have Sweden’s mainstream parties adopted the far right’s policies? The Social Democrats have co-opted their ideas, even though they are counter to the country’s needs. In Sweden, we need competent, talented people who want to come and live here, we need labour for health and social care. Yet nationalism seems to be the prevailing ideology now.”

In a widely read Guardian essay headlined How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, published before the vote, Martin Gelin documented his country’s transformation after 2022. Rightwing parties that year signed a Faustian pact with the Sweden Democrats, buying its support for a minority rightwing government. The deal? The far right was given a direct hand in shaping policy. “A new Sweden has emerged, cruel and cold for migrants”, wrote Gelin, with xenophobic and ethno-nationalist ideas “now comfortably embedded in the political mainstream”.
Most shockingly, Andersson’s Social Democrats, modelling themselves on their hardline Danish counterparts, had bought into the far right’s framings on crime and immigration.

Will Sweden’s Social Democrats now learn from their worst performance in more than 100 years, and embrace an agenda that does not involve deporting toddlers to Iran, people with dementia to the UK, or locking up 14-year-olds?
Jungar is sceptical. “When it comes to linking crime and immigration, this is the new normal,” she said. “The Social Democrats will not pursue policies that are more liberal.”

Yet the political centre in Sweden could articulate a clear alternative to the far right, Mudde says. The Left and the Greens did significantly better among young voters in this week’s election. “This reflects a development we see across Europe, namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties.”
after newsletter promotion
Ghosts of grievance

blocks.caption: Ulrich Siegmund (centre), head of the AfD state parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, celebrates his party’s election win with parliamentary leaders Alice Weidel (left) and Tino Chrupalla (right). Photograph: Michael Kappeler/DPA/AP

blocks.text: Like Giorgia Meloni’s party, Brothers of Italy, and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, the Sweden Democrats have “deradicalised” in selective ways, to broaden their appeal, Jungar told me.
By contrast, what was striking in Germany, was how the AfD doubled its score to 44% of the vote, on what Constanze Stelzenmuller in the FT called “a programme of stunning malevolence”.

Two further regional elections this Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will be closely watched, including by the AfD’s American backers such as Elon Musk. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has economic and demographic conditions comparable to Saxony Anhalt.

For those struggling to understand the appeal of the AfD in eastern Germany, Carolin Würfel’s essay offered an original insight. Born in the former East Germany, Würfel believes that many voters there don’t actually know or care about the AfD’s detailed policies. But the party had tapped into a legacy of grievance about the economic impact of reunification in the 1990s. “Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.” The AfD won’t improve life in east Germany, Würfel wrote, “but that was never the point”.

As in Sweden, the political centre in Germany is now being warned that time is running out to offer a credible democratic alternative to the far right. As Florian Ranft of the Das Progressive Zentrum thinktank wrote: “Waiting for the AfD to fail is not a strategy.”

articles.title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his assassination
articles.summary: The conservative activist was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.

blocks.text: Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event.
In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target.
Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.
The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News.

"We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community."
The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit.
It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him.
"Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges.

"Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says.
Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site.
The family also alleges the university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking.

"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing.
Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial.
Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges.
Prosecutors have called for the death penalty.

articles.title: Burnham warns of ‘difficult decisions’ in budget as inflation rises to 3.1%
articles.summary:
PM rejects claim he leads a ‘tax-and-spend’ government, as Bank of England prepares for interest rates decision

Andy Burnham has said “difficult decisions” will need to be taken in next…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said “difficult decisions” will need to be taken in next month’s budget after a rise in energy prices triggered by the Iran war drove UK inflation above 3%.

In a fresh blow for living standards amid the worsening damage to the global economy from the Middle East conflict, official figures showed soaring fuel prices pushed inflation from 2.9% in July to 3.1% in August.

With the government under pressure as the fallout from the war rattles global financial markets, the prime minister signalled the 28 October budget would take into account investor fears over the hit to the public finances.
“We will take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track,” he said.
“It is going to be challenging, because the picture around the world is challenging, particularly the situation in the Middle East, and we will look carefully at all those things.
“We won’t take risks with people’s living standards or with the economy as a whole, so we will take it all into account.”

The prime minister also downplayed criticism from Andy Haldane, who has urged him not to raise taxes. The former Bank of England chief economist, who advised Burnham before he entered Downing Street, told LBC on Tuesday: “The market now suspects that this is a traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos.”
Burnham rejected that characterisation, saying: “We are not that already … It’s not the case that we aren’t going to take difficult decisions.”

In a critical week for the economy, the Bank of England is preparing for a decision on interest rates on Thursday against the backdrop of rising inflationary pressures from soaring oil and gas prices.

With headline inflation drifting further from its 2% target, financial markets predict a one-in-five chance of a quarter-point rise from the current level of 3.75% as Threadneedle Street comes under pressure to take action. The City expects at least four increases to 4.75% next year.

Economists said there were signs that underlying inflation remained in check amid a cooling UK jobs market. Inflation in the service sector of the economy, which is closely monitored by the Bank, remained unchanged at 3.4%. Core inflation – which excludes volatile items such as energy and food – also held steady at 2.6%.

Official figures on Tuesday showed a slowdown in wage growth and rise in unemployment. The Bank has previously said a cooling jobs market could help limit the risk of stubbornly high inflation becoming entrenched.
However, as the fallout from the Middle East war intensifies, economists said inflation in the UK could continue to climb closer to 4%, heaping pressure on the government and the Bank to take action.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “Given this ramp-up in consumer prices, the pressure on the Bank of England to raise rates is mounting, although a hold at 3.75% is still expected tomorrow.
after newsletter promotion
“It feels like Groundhog Day, with consumers once again feeling the pinch due to geopolitical events far beyond their control.”
As fighting across the Middle East intensifies, the global oil price has soared to more than $106 a barrel.

According to the latest inflation snapshot, the Office for National Statistics said the increase in the headline rate in August was driven by a 23% increase in motor fuel prices. The average petrol price rose by 9.1p between July and August to 161.3p a litre, the highest level since November 2022. Diesel prices rose by 14.2p to 181.8p a litre.

Air fares also rose sharply, with an increase of 6.2% between July and August, particularly for long-haul routes. Rising crude oil and fuel prices also drove up the cost of raw material and the price of goods leaving factories.

The sharp rise in energy prices pushed the European Central Bank to raise interest rates last week, while financial markets predicted the US Federal Reserve would raise borrowing costs on Wednesday for the first time since 2023.

Bond markets have been thrown into a tailspin, with intense selling pressure pushing the yield – in effect the interest rate – on US government bonds above 5% for the first time since 2023 and driving long-term UK government borrowing costs to the highest levels in decades.

The renewed squeeze on the cost of living will intensify the calls on the chancellor, John Healey, to use the 28 October budget to give breathing space to British households reeling from years of soaring prices for energy, food and other everyday items.

Richard Carter, the head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, said: “Today’s figures are a kick in the teeth for an administration that wants to make easing the cost of living its central mission.
“The budget is quickly coming into focus and with borrowing costs continuing to climb for the UK, measures are going to be limited and thus growth will remain challenged.”

articles.title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
articles.summary: Chicago-born playwright Bonnie Greer, who became a familiar face in British political discourse later in life, has died. Her husband David Hutchins announced news of Greer's death.

image.caption: Chicago-born Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and acquired dual citizenship around a decade later [FILE: February 2020]Image: Mark Thomas/i Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media.
A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK.
She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain.

blocks.caption: Greer attended the Frankfurt book fair in 2019 at the height of the post-Brexit debate for a panel on the topicImage: DW/E. Grenier

blocks.text: What did Greer's husband say about her death?

Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life."
Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness.
He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together.
"To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated.

blocks.caption: Greed became a prominent political commentator and activist in the UK [FILE: October 2017]Image: Jonathan Nicholson/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Who was Bonnie Greer?
Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers.
Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings.
She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career.
Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer.
Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities.

She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play.
Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time".

Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time.

She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School.
