articles.title: Gaza: At least 21 dead, including children, in building collapse
articles.summary: The search for survivors has been hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery in the Gaza Strip. Authorities say 2,000 damaged buildings in the territory are occupied by families who have…

image.caption: The search for survivors is ongoing but hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machineryImage: Mahmoud Issa/REUTERS

blocks.text: At least 21 people, including six children, were killed in the Gaza Strip in the early hours of Wednesday morning when a war-damaged building collapsed, injuring at least 14 more people and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.
On Wednesday, rescue workers were still searching through the wreckage — in many cases with their bare hands given the lack of heavy machinery in the devastated Palestinian enclave.

"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble," said Raed Al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, adding that at least 10 families had lived in the collapsed building and expressing hope that more survivors could yet be found.

"My friend and neighbors live in this building," resident Mohannad Al-Mashharawi told the AFP news agency. "I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home."
The death toll is expected to rise as the search for victims buried in the rubble continues.
Gaza: Hundreds of buildings at risk of collapse

"The situation, you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed," said Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations (UN) Development Program's Gaza office. "So there are actually people ​are digging with their bare hands."
With wetter autumn and winter weather approaching, Mrakic warned that rain water could destabilize hundreds of other bombed-out buildings in the war-torn territory.
"There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse," he said. "And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter."

According to authorities, about 2,000 damaged buildings in Gaza are still inhabited by Palestinian families, many of whom have told the Reuters news agency that it is the only way to shelter from the wind and rain in the absence of sufficient tents.

"Today's tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives," said Ramiz Alakbarov, UN Humanitarian ⁠Coordinator for ​the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
"No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter."
Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery
Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery available in the enclave.

Israel says it wants to keep such machines out of the hands of Hamas militants, who used such equipment in their deadly raid into Israel in October 2023, prompting Israel's devastating assault on Gaza which has since killed over 73,000 Palestinians — the vast majority of them civilians.

More than 1,300 Palestinians, also mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since a US-backed ceasefire in October 2025, while the Israeli military says four of its soldiers soldiers have been killed.

articles.title: Forgotten US court of 'secrecy' could mean more deportations
articles.summary: The use of a secretive and long dormant court in the deportation of a woman from the US could have significant consequences. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was just used for the first time in its…

image.caption: The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was used for the first time in three decades Image: Public Domain/U.S. Federal Government

blocks.text: An estimated 4.5 million people have been deported from the US since 1996. But until this month, not one of those cases had involved the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC).

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, from Afghanistan, lived in Texas and had legal US permanent residency. According to a statment released by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Wednesday, she has now returned to Afghanistan after she "conceded she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous status."
"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.
US Senate confirms Trump lawyer Blanche as attorney general
However, Zada's public defenders Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras earlier said that the case "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy."

The court, founded as part of a raft of anti-terror measures after the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, was set up to deal with non-US citizens facing terrorism-related charges on which the evidence is confidential or somehow related to national security.
ATRC never needed before

Hiroshi Motomura, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), told DW that it appears the Donald Trump administration is using the ATRC as the latest tool in its deportation toolkit.

"This is a very elaborate procedure. There are so many other ways that you can essentially get someone out of the United States by using the word terrorism in the context of removal proceedings," he said.
"From a very practical perspective, the government's non-use reflects its view over the last 30 years that 'we don't need this court because we can essentially deport people without it.'"

Zada was accused by prosecutors of being the "matriarch" of a family in which two men — son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhed — had been found guilty of plotting to carry out a mass shooting on election day in 2024. Earlier this year, Blanche described the family as "ISIS-sympathizing."

For Motomura, who has written a number of books and teaches on immigration and citizenship, one of the key distinctions between the ATRC and regular means of deportation is that those on trial do not have a chance to view the evidence against them. Their lawyers may be able to in some cases.
Secrecy inherent in operation of ATRC

"I'm speculating, although I think not unreasonably, that this is someone against whom they cannot invoke terrorism or other grounds without the kind of disclosure in court that they would not want to have," Motomura said.
DHS said in the statement released on Wednesday that they provided Zada and her lawyers with "half a terabyte of documents," though it did not disclose what these showed.

"So they would rather go through a more elaborate procedure and disclose it in chambers to a judge as opposed to having it be potentially more public," Motomura said. "Because the procedure that this court provides is a procedure that calls for some disclosure, but also calls for some secrecy."
The ATRC consists of five federal trial court judges selected by the chief justice of the US Supreme Court, John Roberts, who was appointed by George W. Bush in 2005.

The government must first apply to the court demonstrating it has probable cause to suggest a person is an "alien terrorist" under the immigration law definition. It must also lay out why proceeding through standard deportation procedures would be a national security risk. In Zada's case this happened in July.

Then comes the hearing, in which the government need only prove their case "by the preponderance of the evidence", a lower bar than usually applied to such cases. Zada's decision to leave the country without the hearing means that the feasibility of the government using the court in future remains somewhat in the balance due to a constitutional point that was not tested.
Due process constitutional question yet to be resolved

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process. We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue," said Zada's lawyers in a statement to the Washington Post.

blocks.caption: US Attorney General Todd Blanche hailed the deportation as a "win for national security"Image: Rod Lamkey/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: An amendment to the US constitution states that no state can "deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." Whether this applies in cases such as Zada's is not yet clear, something Motomura said may frustrate the Trump administration.

"I bet they were disappointed. I don't know this, but it would not surprise me if they're disappointed that the case never got litigated in court on the constitutional issue because it would allow them a different opportunity to limit the rights of people in the United States under the US Constitution," he said.

Given the Trump administration's stated "zero tolerance" policy on immigration — which has also included deporting people to so-called ‘third countries' they have no connection with and the widespread deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents — it seems likely it won't be 30 years before another case is brought before the ATRC. And that could have significant implications for justice.

"I think it's very hard to view this situation accurately without seeing it as part of a broader effort by the administration to limit access to courts and to legal counsel and access to evidence on multiple fronts," concluded Motomura.

articles.title: Allies, victims' families react to Rodrigo Duterte's first in-person ICC appearance
articles.summary: Allies of former President Rodrigo Duterte and families of victims of his administration"s war on drugs reacted to his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 11:03pm
Allies of former President Rodrigo Duterte and families of victims of his administration’s war on drugs reacted to his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court on Wednesday.
Dressed in a black suit and white shirt, Duterte attended the third status conference in his crimes against humanity case as part of preparations for his trial, which is set to begin on November 30.
Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague on March 12, 2025. He last appeared before the ICC via video link on March 14, 2025.
On Facebook, Senator Robin Padilla posted photos of Duterte’s appearance before Trial Chamber III, captioned simply, “Tatay.”
Senator Christopher “Bong” Go, who served as Duterte’s aide for more than two decades, also posted images from the status conference, captioned, “Tatay Digong.”

“We’re happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight,” said Llore Pasco, whose two sons were killed during Duterte’s war on drugs, as she watched a television broadcast of the hearing from Manila.

“When I saw Duterte’s face, I felt a sense of relief, knowing that he is still there in The Hague. He cannot leave. Thank you to the ICC for taking care of Duterte there for us so that we can achieve true justice,” said Sally Ramos, the mother of another drug war casualty, in a report by Raffy Tima on “24 Oras.”
In January, ICC judges said Duterte’s health was good enough for him to follow the proceedings and requested that he appear in court in person rather than via video link from the detention unit.

The warrant for Duterte’s arrest says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including during his time as mayor of Davao City.
Police said 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations, but human rights groups said the actual number could be higher.

Duterte said he had instructed police to act in self-defense and told supporters he was ready to “rot in jail” if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs. —with a report from Reuters/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Panganiban makes 'binata' quip as Hontiveros questions him
articles.summary: Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban directed a flirtatious remark at Sen. Risa Hontiveros as the latter questioned him during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 11:02pm

Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban on Wednesday directed a flirtatious remark at Senator Risa Hontiveros as the latter questioned him during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Panganiban was appearing at the Senate court as one of the four amici curiae invited to weigh in on the conviction threshold of the impeachment court.
During her questioning, Hontiveros said that Panganiban was free to answer questions she would be asking to the other experts.
Panganiban said that he would even entertain Hontiveros’ questions in private.

“Maski po sa pribado na conversation natin, pwede ako sumagot… dalaga naman po kayo,” the 88-year-old joked with a smile. (Even in private we can have a conversation, I can answer… after all, you are unmarried.)
Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero then jokingly asked Hontiveros: “Can you confirm?”
Hontiveros chose to laugh it off. "Ibang mga tanong pa po ang itatanong ko, Mr. Presiding Officer, sa ating mga amicus curiae," she said.
(I have other questions to ask the other amici curiae.)
“Di ko rin nasabi, binata rin ako,” Panganiban added, laughing. (I was not able to say it but I am a bachelor.)
“I’m sure marami po nagno-note niyan,” Hontiveros replied. (I’m sure plenty are taking note.)

Both Panganiban and Hontiveros are widowed. Panganiban lost his wife, Professor Elenita Carpio-Panganiban, in 2023 after 62 years of marriage, while Hontiveros, who lost her husband Francisco Baraquel Jr. in 2005, said she has a longtime partner. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Health officials in turmoil over 11th-hour backflip on aged care algorithm override powers, emails reveal
articles.summary:
Ministers given emergency briefing about changes to algorithm decisions just three days before tool rollout

  • Get our

blocks.text: Senior department of health officials were in turmoil before the rollout of an algorithm to determine funding packages for older Australians, after discovering legislation had been drafted so rigidly that the tool could not legally be overridden by aged care assessors.

Emails published under freedom of information (FoI) by the department of health, disability and ageing show that, despite assessors long receiving reassurance from the department that they would have powers to change incorrect algorithm decisions, officials realised at the 11th hour this would violate proposed regulations.

It prompted an emergency briefing of the aged care minister Sam Rae and health minister Mark Butler just three days before the rollout of the algorithm. In an email, they were warned by senior department staff that removing the human override function from the aged care assessment tool for support at home (SaH) packages carried risk.

blocks.caption: The federal minister for health, Mark Butler. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

blocks.text: In the email sent on 29 October, three days before the 1 November algorithm rollout, the ministers were told: “There is a risk that this late change in messaging to assessment organisations may not filter through to assessor behaviour.

“In public statements, including responses to media enquiries, the department has regularly indicated that there will be an ability for assessors to override the … classification algorithm recommendation. In accordance with this position, an override functionality has been built into the relevant systems.”

However, the ministers were told the Aged Care Rules 2025 legislation had been drafted in a way that provided “no legal discretion for assessors or assessment delegates to override the recommendation of the algorithm for a SaH classification”.

It meant the manual for using the algorithm and the assessment tool it was part of – known as the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) – needed to be updated ahead of the rollout to make it clear to assessors that they could not override outcomes.
“Assessment organisations (including state and territory governments) or individual assessors may criticise this position as being inconsistent with previous government statements,” the email said.

The IAT involves an assessor asking an older person questions about their physical, social and personal circumstances before the algorithm uses this data to determine how much government-funded home support and funding they are eligible to receive.
The algorithmic decision cannot be overridden by the assessor even if they believe the older person has been allocated a lower level of support than needed.

On 24 October an assistant secretary at the department, Rachel Blackwood, wrote to deputy secretary of aged care Greg Pugh about the legal issues that had come to light around allowing assessors to override the algorithm.
The Aged Care Rules 2025 “have been drafted to provide no discretion for assessors or assessment delegates to do anything other than accept the recommendation of the SaH algorithm,” her email said.

Blackwood wrote that the department had “consistently indicated that assessment delegates would have the discretion to use their clinical judgement to override the recommendation of the SaH algorithm”.
“It is clear that the inclusion of an override has been regarded by many staff … as a settled position.”
She presented a list of solutions and risks, all of which were redacted in the FoI documents. On 26 October, Pugh responded that the solution he had chosen “… may not be your preferred approach”.

“However I am comfortable that this decision is the best available in light of all contextual circumstances, including proximity to 1 November and having a clear and workable pathway to address it,” he wrote. “A big thanks for working through this tricky issue and for providing your frank and open advice.”

On 27 October, Blackwood wrote to Pugh: “We have been working hard to build credibility with assessment organisations and other stakeholders, and want to avoid doing things that will undermine our working relationship at a critical time.
“We have a responsibility to provide guidance to delegates to exercise their powers with integrity, accuracy and honesty,” she wrote.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Guardian Australia previously reported that people already on support packages who needed reassessment because of increased needs were routinely being recommended for less support by the algorithm. Photograph: The Good Brigade/Getty Images

blocks.text: It is unclear why the department chose to remove assessor override from the instruction manual, rather than change the legislation to allow override. The department of health did not respond to requests for comment.

Within days of the algorithm rollout, Blackwood was emailing other senior department officials to say complaints were coming in from distressed assessors that the algorithm was routinely under-assessing vulnerable older Australians, leaving them without adequate support.

In an email to senior department staff sent on 20 November Blackwood wrote; “The majority of Aged Care Needs Assessment Organisations (including State and Territory Governments) have raised concerns about the inability to override the IAT classification algorithm”.
“Assessment organisations have provided details of cases in which assessors believe the algorithm has generated an outcome that does not align with client needs,” she wrote.
Separate documents released to Guardian Australia under FoI show state health officials were keeping logs of hundreds of cases of underassessment, sending these to their federal counterparts.

“Approving classifications and assessment outcomes that they [aged care assessors] do not agree with does not align with their professional ethics and they are concerned this has possible legal impacts,” one of those emails, sent on 14 November, said.

Guardian Australia previously reported that people already on support packages who needed reassessment because their needs had increased were routinely being recommended for lower support packages by the algorithm.

FoI documents also reveal that when the department discovered the tool was under-assessing people despite the government’s public promises and policy that older Australians would be “no worse off” under the aged care reforms, a workaround was implemented.

When an aged care assessor clicked “accept” on the algorithm’s downgraded package recommendation, the portal temporarily kept the client’s old package dollar amount active while quietly logging a lower clinical classification on their permanent record, the documents show.
The shadow aged care minister, Anne Ruston, said the Coalition had introduced legislation to restore human decision-making to the assessment process and accused Labor from blocking it.
She described it as “a practical, overdue fix that has passed the Senate but remains blocked by Labor from even being debated in the House”.
Ruston said while restoring the override was necessary, it was nowhere near sufficient on its own to fix an aged care system she described as “broken”.
Do you know more? melissa.davey@theguardian.com

articles.title: Labor seats get more than 90% of funding distributed under controversial multi-million dollar grants program
articles.summary:
Guardian Australia analysis adds to concerns over the federal scheme, which is to be the subject of a Senate inquiry

Federal Labor seats have received over 90% of funds already awarded in…
articles.byline: Luca Ittimani, Sarah Basford Canales and Benita Kolovos

blocks.text: Federal Labor seats have received over 90% of funds already awarded in the first five months of a controversial multi-million dollar grants program, adding to concerns over the scheme’s selection process.

The $568m community grants scheme will be the subject of a Senate inquiry after a report by the Centre for Public Integrity last week revealed the scheme favoured projects in notionally Labor-held electorates, including a $6m grant for a golf club in Anthony Albanese’s electorate.

The report dealt with the allocation of the funds. Now Guardian Australia analysis shows the money so far distributed by the scheme has been even more heavily skewed toward Labor seats, which have received 92% of approved funding.

In a sign the federal government is delivering funding to Victoria faster than other states, Victoria’s share of approvals exceeded its share of the overall allocations. The opposition has accused the government of propping up its state Labor counterparts in an attempt to save “political furniture”.
Labor invited councils to formally apply for the Major and Local Community Infrastructure program late last year, with the infrastructure department approving $248m of projects since March.
The figures show Victoria and New South Wales were the biggest state recipients of the non-competitive grants program, receiving $189.7m.

Councils in Victoria – where a state election is fast approaching – have so far received $99m, with $92m worth of projects located in seats held by state Labor MPs, including a number at risk of defeat at the polls in November.

The single biggest grant delivered by the Albanese government’s program was $25m for the new Bacchus Marsh aquatic centre in the respective federal and state Labor seats of Hawke and Eureka. Eureka is under threat from One Nation, as is Bendigo West, which has been approved for nearly $7m from the same scheme.
Another $106m was promised to Victoria ahead of the 2025 federal election but is yet to be formally approved.
NSW’s Lake Macquarie council was allocated the most individual grants, with 13 upgrades to sports fields and lighting worth a combined $8.8m, all of which have been approved.
The council covers NSW state Labor seats and an independent seat. NSW Labor is up for re-election in March 2027.
Western Australia, Tasmania and Queensland have been been approved for less than $25m, $15m and $8m respectively to date. Each has been promised close to $50m.
Helen Haines, the independent MP for the federal seat of Indi in rural Victoria, said governments should invest in local communities but “election should not be the selection”.
“Public money should go where there is genuine community need and demonstrated merit - not where it delivers political advantage,” she said.

The Albanese government has described the structure of the grants program as “sound” and claimed there were no conflicts of interest given final decisions were made by the infrastructure minister, not local MPs or proponents.
But the minister, Catherine King, did not directly answer when asked how projects were selected or approved, or whether their location in state or federal Labor seats was considered.

“The Major and Local Community Infrastructure program (MLCIP) delivers the election commitments made by the Australian Labor Party through a one-off, closed, non-competitive grant program, in line with longstanding practice,” King said.
“The guidelines explicitly state that applications which do not meet [specific] benchmarks will not be considered value for money and will not be awarded funding.”
The Senate will hold an inquiry into the scheme over the next two months, proposed by the Greens with Coalition with crossbench support. Labor voted against the inquiry on Monday.
The Greens spokesperson for democracy, senator Steph Hodgins-May, said it would investigate how projects were selected, who was locked out and whether conflicts of interest were properly declared.

“The public deserves to know how their money was allocated, who made the decisions and whether everyone got a fair go,” Hodgins-May said. “I expect Labor to stop hiding behind their talking points and front up to this inquiry.”
Victorian wishlists
The Victorian state Labor government is approaching the poll with less cash to spend than in previous campaigns.

Before the May budget, Labor MPs were told to identify smaller local projects they would like to see funded by the state in their electorate. In the previous budget, they were given a spending cap and asked to limit their list to five items.
Victorian Labor sources have confirmed that MPs were told to be “realistic” with their campaign wishlists and to include price points.
“Each MP has a wishlist, will they get everything on it? Probably not,” one source, not authorised to speak publicly, said.
Another said: “It’s not going to be a spendathon.”
Some MPs have also banded together to jointly bid for state funding for projects that span electorates.
The Victorian premier’s office was approached for comment but did not respond.
The sources stressed the shift was due to the tightening fiscal environment and the leadership of the new premier, Ben Carroll, who has pledged to “respect” taxpayer funds.

With state debt forecast to soar to $199bn in 2029/2030 and AI-generated ads from the political lobby group Fix Victoria depicting a “debt tsunami,” sources said voters commonly raised the issue during door knocking.
One source said the state government had “no influence” or involvement in the grants being distributed at a federal level.
The federal Victorian senator James Paterson said taxpayer money was being used to prop up Albanese’s “mate”, Carroll.
“It was bad enough already that federal Labor was prepared to use public money in such a nakedly partisan way for their own electoral benefit,” Paterson said.
“Federal grants shouldn’t be used to try to save Victorian Labor’s political furniture.”

articles.title: ‘Godfather of AI’ says tech regulation is nearing Covid-style pivot moment
articles.summary:
Safety crisis makes it more likely that governments will be spurred into action, says Yoshua Bengio

Concerns over AI safety are reaching a point where governments realise they must act to…

blocks.text: Concerns over AI safety are reaching a point where governments realise they must act to protect the public, similarly to in the Covid pandemic, according to one of the “godfathers” of the technology.

Yoshua Bengio said recent events, including a “swarm” of OpenAI agents hacking a startup and tech insider warnings of an existential threat, were cutting through – making government action more likely.
The Canadian computer scientist, a prominent voice in the campaign to rein in breakneck AI development, said he was now “more optimistic than many observers because I see the public moving”.

Comparing the AI safety crisis to the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020, Bengio said: “Think about how quickly governments moved after the beginning of the pandemic when they realised that public safety, their future, democracy, was in danger. You would expect that they move quickly. So we are, I think, nearing that point.”

Concern over the potential threat of powerful AI systems has reached a new pitch in recent months after a series of safety incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic agents carrying out unsanctioned activities such as hacking third parties, hijacking a German website, and using fake identities to try to trick developers.

His comments came as 42 fellows and foreign members of the Royal Society wrote to the organisation’s president, Sir Paul Nurse, to express their “extreme concern” over the pace of AI development. “By the time the situation becomes obvious to the wider public, it may be too late to act,” the researchers wrote in an open letter to Nurse. “We believe this is an emergency, and call on the Royal Society to use its influence to convey this view to government and the media.”

Last week, a researcher at Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot, resigned after warning that colleagues believed AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade”. Days later, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, called for a slowdown in the pace of cutting-edge AI development – a move that was immediately supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX.

However, sceptics of the “slowdown” call have claimed that calls by major AI firms are an example of “regulatory capture”, where companies persuade governments to introduce safety regimes that raise the cost of smaller rivals being able to compete. They also claim existential fears overshadow more immediate issues with AI such as its impact on copyright-protected work and human rights.

Bengio said he disagreed with the regulatory capture argument because a slowdown by leading AI firms would “cost them financially”. The US president, Donald Trump, has rejected a slowdown, saying he does not want the US to lose its lead over China in the AI race.

blocks.caption: Yoshua Bengio, a professor at the University of Montreal, won a Turing award in 2018.  Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Bengio spoke as the Canadian and German governments announced funding of up to C$300m (£160m) for his non-profit organisation dedicated to creating an “honest AI” that will act as a guardrail against rogue agents – AI tools that carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention.

Bengio, a professor at the University of Montreal, earned the “godfather of AI” moniker after winning the 2018 Turing award, seen as the equivalent of a Nobel prize for computing. He shared it with Geoffrey Hinton, who later won a Nobel, and Yann LeCun, the former chief AI scientist at Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta.

Bengio’s organisation, LawZero, is developing a system called Scientist AI that will act as a guardrail against AI agents showing deceptive or self-preserving behaviour, such as trying to avoid being turned off. LawZero is also funded by the Gates Foundation, the chipmaker Nvidia, and Coefficient Giving, a philanthropic body linked to effective altruism, a movement that believes AI poses an existential threat.

The LawZero technology is viewed by Bengio as a counterpoint to reinforcement learning, a trial-and-error development technique used by major AI companies where AIs are rewarded for working out how to carry out a specific task. The Canadian computer scientist believes, along with other experts, this training technique encourages AIs to pursue their goals recklessly and cause harm in the process, as shown by the OpenAI “swarm”.

Deployed alongside an AI agent, Bengio’s technology would raise potentially harmful behaviour by an autonomous system – having weighed whether its actions could cause harm. Bengio expects the technology to be deployed for other uses eventually, such as accelerating scientific breakthroughs.

articles.title: Divine Adili’s parents accept teammates’ account on son’s death: ‘We have known the truth’
articles.summary: Seeking answers, Elias and Ifeoma Adili visit the Philippines for the first time and hear firsthand from Divine's teammates what happened in the June 8 incident that claimed the lives of their son…

blocks.text: PRESENT. Divine Adili's parents, Elias and Ifeoma, watch the Ateneo Blue Eagles in UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament game.
UAAP

Seeking answers, Elias and Ifeoma Adili visit the Philippines for the first time and hear firsthand from Divine's teammates what happened in the June 8 incident that claimed the lives of their son and Rene Baterbonia

items: Elias and Ifeoma Adili visited the Philippines to learn the truth about their son Divine's death during a team building on June 8.
They attended a basketball game where they felt a bittersweet connection to their son, who had promised to bring them to watch him play.

Despite their grief, the Adilis are determined to move forward, acknowledging the difficulty of their loss and expressing disappointment over the delayed communication from the former Ateneo head coach.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The parents of late Ateneo big man Divine Adili can return home to Nigeria having known the “truth” about their son’s death.

Visiting the country for the first time in search of answers, Elias and Ifeoma Adili heard firsthand from Divine’s teammates what happened during the June 8 incident that claimed the lives of their son and Rene Baterbonia during a team-building activity in Dipaculao, Aurora.

“We talked to the teammates, because they are the ones that will tell us what happened, because they were present at the place of the scene. So they explained everything,” Elias said. “That was our purpose of coming — to see the team, to talk with them, to tell us the truth.”
“It’s only the truth that will set you free. Okay? So we have known the truth and I think I can now go back to my kinsmen and tell them that this is what happened.”

blocks.caption: Divine Adili’s parents accept teammates’ account on son’s death: ‘We have known the truth’

blocks.text: Elias and Ifeoma were in attendance as the Blue Eagles opened their UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball campaign at the Mall of Asia Arena on Wednesday, September 16, exactly 100 days since the two student-athletes’ deaths.
And Ateneo did not disappoint, breezing past the UE Red Warriors in a 101-74 rout starring Kieffer Alas, Jared Bahay, and Grayson Rogers.
While they are grateful to finally see their son’s team play in person, the moment is inevitably bittersweet for the Adilis.
Divine, after all, had once promised to bring Elias and Ifeoma to the Philippines so they could watch him in action for the Blue Eagles — a commitment that, in the end, was never fulfilled.

“I’m delighted to be here, but I wish I am watching my son. But I really appreciate what I see because I know that my son is there. Divine and Rene, they are there. They might be invisible, but I know my son is there,” said Ifeoma.

“I wish to come to the Philippines to watch my son play because that’s what I’ve been desiring. And I know my son desired that, to bring us to the Philippines to come and watch him live, though we have been watching his games [online]. We have been watching every of his games since he came to the Philippines and he desired to bring us here.”
Moving on has also been particularly difficult for the Adilis, especially now that they find themselves surrounded by things and people that were once close to their son.

“To be honest with you, it has not been easy. I tried to move on. But honestly, it has not been easy for me. Even as I entered the Philippines, the moment I stepped in at the airport, I felt so emotional,” said Ifeoma. “I don’t want to cry. But unfortunately today, the moment I stepped into the playground, I saw myself crying. But it’s fine.”
Ifeoma also expressed her disappointment that former Ateneo head coach Tab Baldwin only reached out to their family much later.

“He spoke to us very late, about four days after the incident, which is not proper,” said Ifeoma. “I am not okay with that. To be honest with you, since then, we’ve not heard from him. And it’s okay, it’s okay.”
As painful as Divine’s death is, though, the Adilis know they have to live with it and find the strength to move forward without their son.

“There’s nothing we can do. We can’t bring him back. We have cried, we have shed tears, we have complained. But there’s nothing we can do. Thank God we saw his remains — seeing his remains and laying him to rest,” said Elias.
Elias and Ifeoma will also be around when the Blue Eagles battle perennial finalist UP Fighting Maroons on Saturday, September 19, at the Araneta Coliseum. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US officials decide against backing Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders
articles.summary:
Armed group appears to reach agreement with Trump administration over safety of Red Sea shipping

Officials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat,…

blocks.text: Officials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat, Oman, it has been confirmed, leading to the US decision not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back a Houthi advance inside Yemen.

The Houthis reassured the US that the ceasefire agreement between the two sides struck in 2025 still held and the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. Only Saudi-linked shipping was regarded as a target owing to its blockade of Yemen, the Houthis confirmed.

The meeting helps to explain the decision from the US president, Donald Trump, to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in an expensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis.

The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past has met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president JD Vance confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis.

The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure on Saudi Arabia to reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast.

The former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding between the Trump administration and the Houthis” had been struck. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.”

In a bid to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the controversial claim that the Houthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said in a statement.

Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca is a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognised Yemen government based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X.

Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, adding that such worn-out lies had been used before and had fooled no one.

The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid Abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”.

The Houthis countered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed Abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda.

Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals.

“Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.”

Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran. The report from Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the commander of US Central Command (Centcom), Adm Brad Cooper.
after newsletter promotion

Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since the US and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.

A meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country.

In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in a bid to secure Chinese support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains effectively closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China does not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on the memorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country.
Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a key Saudi East-West pipeline remains closed because of a bombing incident.

articles.title: St. John's woman with 160 prior convictions, including for fraud and forgery, gets jail time in CERB case
articles.summary: After several trial delays, former housing advocate Michelle Voisey is headed back to prison after pleading guilty to fraud.

image.caption: Michelle Voisey, seen here in a file photo, has been sentenced to 10 months in jail for using her niece's CRA account to send herself $8,000 in CERB payments. (Mark Cumby/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
After several trial delays, former housing advocate Michelle Voisey is headed back to prison after pleading guilty to fraud.
Michelle Voisey has been handed a 10-month jail sentence
A former St. John’s housing advocate is returning to jail for the latest in a long list of criminal convictions.

Michelle Voisey was handed a 10-month sentence with 24 months probation for using her niece’s Canada Revenue Agency account to send $8,000 worth of Canada Emergency Response Benefit payments to her own bank account.
The federal program, known as CERB, provided financial support to people who lost their jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic.

items: St. John's housing advocate pleads guilty to fraud, but legal aid request delays sentencing
Sentencing of St. John's serial fraudster and former housing advocate delayed again

blocks.text: “The seriousness of the offence lies not only within the amount taken, but also its deliberate nature, the abuse of trust, the impact on the victim and Ms. Voisey’s extensive history of similar offending,” Justice Peter Browne said at Voisey’s sentencing hearing in Supreme Court in St. John's on Sept. 11.
Former St. John’s housing advocate gets jail sentence for fraud

Browne ordered Voisey to repay the $8,000 to CRA, and banned her from holding any job or volunteer position where she would have authority over another person's property or money for a period of 20 years.

Browne said Voisey’s decision to plead guilty was a mitigating factor in his decision, though he also considered her criminal history. Voisey has nearly 160 previous convictions, many involving fraud, forgery or theft.
“This record demonstrates a long standing and deeply entrenched pattern of dishonest conduct,” Browne said.
Voisey charged back in 2021

According to the statement of facts, Voisey's niece contacted police when her GST payment didn't arrive on time. She learned that $8,000 in CERB payments had been paid out in her name — even though she hadn't applied and didn't qualify for the benefit. Voisey was charged in October 2021.

In 2023, while the case was winding its way through court, Voisey, operating under the name Michelle Gushue, participated in the tent city protest on Confederation Hill. Voisey participated in media interviews and solicited donations of gift cards, cell phones, cash and more through social media.
Voisey’s latest conviction is unrelated to the tent city protest.
Voisey pleaded guilty in June 2025, but a last-minute request for a legal aid lawyer delayed sentencing until 2026.

items: St. John's housing advocate pleads guilty to fraud, but legal aid request delays sentencing
Sentencing of St. John's serial fraudster and former housing advocate delayed again

blocks.text: At Friday’s sentencing, Voisey’s lawyer, Dan Furey, submitted a letter he said is from her family doctor, indicating that she's been diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Browne declined to take the letter into consideration in sentencing, explaining that the defence would need to make an oral application and call in an expert witness, like an oncologist.
“I'm not prepared to entertain any of that without expert evidence and in this courtroom to know if incarceration would affect any type of [...] treatment,” he said.

Furey declined to make the application and the sentencing proceeded. After the sentence was handed down, Voisey asked if she could still make the application, but Browne said no. She asked for her sentence to be delayed for two days, but Browne denied that request too.
CBC News has asked Furey if Voisey intends to appeal her sentence.

articles.title: Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over future
articles.summary: Christian Democratic Union leadership throws its weight behind the chancellor ahead of two state elections this weekend.

blocks.text: The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future.

The premiers - all of whom are part of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) - wrote that restoring trust in their party lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel".

Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months, is facing poor approval ratings while the anti-immigration, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is surging, prompting questions about whether he is an electoral liability.
He has vowed to carry on but two more state elections on Sunday have been seen as a key test of his leadership.

Rumours of a "Kanzlertausch" - or "Chancellor swap" - have been around for months, but they have increased since the conservative CDU tumbled to a distant second behind the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt at the start of September.
The AfD shot up to 43.8% of the vote while the CDU plummeted to 17.2%, marking the first time since World War Two that a far-right party has come close to controlling a German state.
It is still three seats short of an outright majority and the major parties would not enter into a coalition with the AfD, though it could seek to form a minority government.

Merz came out fighting after the loss, describing the AfD - which wants to rebuild ties with Russia - as a "destructive force" whose migration policy amounted to an "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers.
The AfD responded to his remarks by saying it was filing a defamation complaint against the chancellor over what it described as "baseless" and "disgusting" claims.

The chancellor's abrasive communication style and personal unpopularity - with just 14% thinking he is right for the job, according to a recent Bild poll - have raised questions about his viability as leader of both Germany and the CDU.
The CDU's eight state premiers wrote, however, that "now more than ever, ⁠Germany's political landscape needs stability".

"Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag [German parliament]," said the leaders of Schleswig-Holstein, Saxony, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia.
It comes after Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria and leader of the CDU's sister party the CSU, stood by Merz.

An unnamed party source told news agency Reuters that CDU officials will meet on Sunday to co-ordinate the party's response to the results of that day's state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania - where the AfD is poised for further gains and the CDU for further losses.

However, the race is far more evenly split in the German capital than it was in Saxony-Anhalt, with the CDU and Die Linke (The Left) vying for first place, and the AfD and Greens not far behind, according to polls.
In Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, polls put the AfD ahead of the centre-left SPD but likely well short of an outright majority.
The worst-case scenario for Merz would be for the CDU to lose power in Berlin and not get enough votes to even have a presence in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania's parliament.

Unlike in the UK, Germany is not well-versed in replacing its leader mid-term, though Merz could, in theory, be pressured to resign or face a vote of no confidence, though many regard that outcome as unlikely.

No one within the CDU has yet said they were willing to challenge Merz, but the speculation about his future has led to several names - including Söder, North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik Wüst and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt - being touted as potential successors.

Even before Merz had officially been made chancellor, he managed to rally support for a massive €500bn ($547bn; £420bn) defence infrastructure fund, with his straight-talking style and focus on European security earning him plaudits on the world stage.

But it took him three attempts to become CDU leader and he then lost an initial vote to become chancellor despite technically having sufficient votes through a coalition deal with the SPD. It was a first in post-war Germany.
This suggests that he has a history of struggling to appeal to even those within his own ranks - and that he may be unlikely to let go of a job he has long coveted.

articles.title: Union claims victory as ministers agree to fully fund pay rise for teachers in England
articles.summary:
National Education Union welcomes news that schools will not have to partly fund increase from their own budgets

The UK’s biggest education union is claiming a major victory after the…

blocks.text: The UK’s biggest education union is claiming a significant victory after the government bowed to pressure and agreed to fully fund a forthcoming pay increase for teachers in England in a sudden U-turn.

Members of the National Education Union (NEU) were due to vote in a ballot for strike action next month over the government’s recent pay offer which provided for a 3.5% increase from this month, with an additional 3% from next September.

While the offer was a significant improvement on initial proposals from the then education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, there was concern among teachers and unions that it was not fully funded and schools would have to find almost a third of the wage increases from existing budgets.

After weeks of negotiation over the summer with the NEU general secretary, Daniel Kebede, Phillipson’s successor, Lucy Powell, confirmed on Monday in a letter to the union that the entire pay offer would be fully funded, using funds from recent revaluations of the local government pension scheme.
Kebede said it was a “significant” step and would result in an estimated additional £500m of funding for schools this year, which otherwise would have been spent on the pay rise.

“Finally, we have a government that accepts the reality that any teacher pay award must be fully funded,” he said. “Plugging the £460m black hole in school budgets signals a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community.

“Schools have been running on empty for far too long. Leaders simply could not afford to fund the pay award as set out by the previous education secretary. The new administration has accepted that it is wrong to force schools to make cuts to education just to make ends meet.”

Although the NEU national executive is yet to decide on the fate of the national ballot, the government will be hoping its latest gesture will lift the threat of strike action and possible school closure across the country.

In a snap poll before the summer break, 97% of NEU members who participated said it was “unacceptable” that their school would have to find the funds to make up the 1.1% shortfall in government funding of the pay rise, and 89% were prepared to take strike action to ensure the teacher pay award was fully funded.
In her letter to Kebede, Powell said: “I understand you are concerned the funding available in 26-27 is insufficient to cover the costs of the recent pay award.

“I am therefore pleased to be able to update you that recent revaluations to the local government pension scheme will see a 4.9ppt reduction in employer contribution rates and deliver significant savings on schools’ pay bill for support staff.
“We can confirm this reduction in costs will not be clawed back and as such, we are confident that schools will be able to cover the costs of the teacher pay award, at a national level.”
She added: “Given the material change to the affordability position, I would ask that the NEU revisits its proposed ballot of members planned for October and moves away from strike action.”
The Department for Education has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: EU moves closer to social media ban for under 13s
articles.summary:
Ursula von der Leyen announces draft law to stop apps ‘depriving children of their childhood’

The EU will move forward with

blocks.text: The EU will move forward with plans for an under 13s social media ban, the head of the European Commission has confirmed.
Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday that social media apps were “depriving children of their childhood” and that big tech platforms needed to prove the safety of their products.
She promised a draft law for a total ban on social media for under 13s, while children aged 13-15 would be allowed “mini accounts” under parental supervision with time limits on apps.
The commission will publish its social media plan on Thursday, which will have to be agreed by the European parliament and 27 EU member states if it is to become law.

Von der Leyen also promised that the commission’s Digital Fairness Act, due to be submitted to the European parliament later this year, would tackle features such as addictive design, which, she said was “harming everyone”.

The commission president made the comments in Strasbourg as part of her annual state of the union address. In a wide-ranging speech covering the EU’s place in a turbulent world and plans for continent-wide legislation, she also promised a European heatwave plan and committed to an emergency response mechanism to deal with sudden inflows of migrants, in response to events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in August.

Invoking “an openly hostile world”, von der Leyen went on to make an unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, and pledged to set out ideas for a European security council involving Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the UK.

The former German defence minister said the EU needed its version of Nato’s article 4 – an “emergency security protocol” that means all member states would convene at the request of another in response to a hybrid attack.

“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she argued. “We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents – those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security.”

Nato’s article 4, which is separate from the collective defence clause, article 5, means members of the alliance can consult when one of them believes their territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.
after newsletter promotion
European nations have recently faced a series of hostile acts attributed to Russia, including sabotage, incursions by jets into European airspace and a drone attack on Leipzig airport.

Warning that Ukraine faced a tough winter, von der Leyen suggested the EU may have reached its limits on economic restrictions against Russia. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she said.
After 21 rounds of measures, EU member states have found it increasingly difficult to agree sanctions on the Kremlin’s war machine, wary of the cost to their own economies.

Von der Leyen also touched on Europe’s divisions over whether or not to introduce restrictions on trade with Israel and its illegal settlements in the West Bank. The commission has declined to publish a proposal to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements, though several EU member states and allies including France, Canada and the UK have moved in this direction.
“When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she said.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 26: 3 ex-SC chief justices say 16-vote threshold can be changed
articles.summary: The amici curiae, or “friends of the court,” took center stage on the 26th day of Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial, with three of the four legal experts saying the Senate impeachment…

blocks.text: The amici curiae, or “friends of the court,” took center stage on the 26th day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, with three of the four legal experts saying the Senate impeachment court can change the 16-vote threshold for conviction, citing the Senate’s authority to try and decide impeachment cases. Their position came amid the continued absence of at least four of the 24 senator-judges.

Former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court Hilario Davide, Jr., Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno all said that the Constitutional provision stating that two-thirds of all the members of the Senate are needed to secure a conviction must not be taken literally since the language used was not a number but a fraction.

“We have decisions of the Supreme Court which clearly decree that public officers facing criminal cases in court cannot, during the pendency of their cases, practice their profession nor hold office, elective or appointive, while in detention. Clearly then, the basis of computing the two-thirds must be the number of senators who are qualified to vote, not the 24 in the present Senate,” Davide said in a written submission.

“Meaningful adjudication requires active participation in the search for truth and fairness. It is only in this manner that a verdict that is fair to the parties, fair to the Senators, and ultimately fair to our sovereign people,” Panganiban added.

Puno, for his part, said, “by using two-thirds, the number of votes to convict will have to move depending on certain factors” because “a strict, standalone, literal interpretation of Article XI Section 3.6 may result in absurdities and may result in injustices which will defeat the purpose of the Constitution.”
It was only retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna who said every member of the Senate should be counted in determining the threshold for conviction.
"As long as he is a member of the Senate he has to be included in the two-thirds denominator. The only exception is if he dies, if he is removed from office, or if he resigns. No more," Azcuna said.
Panganiban and Puno, however, clarified that the decision to determine the threshold solely belongs to the Senate since the Constitution vests that power in them.

“That is why I explained the Senate impeachment court is not under the Supreme Court. If the Constitution wanted the Supreme Court to decide on impeachment cases, then the Senate impeachment court should have been listed under Article VIII of the Constitution on the Judiciary, not Article XI, which is Accountability of Public Officers,” Puno said.

“You (the Senate impeachment court) are an independent, free court. The Constitution said the Senate shall be the sole judge to try and decide impeachment cases. What the Constitution requires is for you, as elected representatives of the people, to make the decision. Not the Supreme Court,” Panganiban added.
Puno also said that the Senate impeachment court is not under the Supreme Court.

As to the invocation of the Avelino v. Cuenco Supreme Court decision, which excluded senators beyond the Senate's coercive jurisdiction from the official count for quorum, Panganiban, Puno and Davide all agreed that this does not directly apply to the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte because the case decided the quorum needs to pass legislation, not the threshold needed to convict and impeachable official.
Justice over legalism

But for Panganiban, justice should prevail over technicalities. As such, he was firm that allowing absent judges to vote or be included in the determination of the voting threshold will be unfair, if not an injustice, to the Filipino public who elected the Senators in the first place.
“I'm talking about justice for our people. What do our people expect from you [Senators]? It's not legalism, it's not judicial conduct. It is justice for our people,” Panganiban said.

“Kesyo dalawampu kayo, dalawampu’t apat kayo, dalawa lang kayo…ang hinahanap po ng ating bayan ay hustisya mula sa Senado. Hindi po pinakikialaman siguro ng mga tao kung sino ang nagbigay ng hustisya. Para sa kanila, meron ba silang hustisya na nakikita, na nararamdaman? I speak from the point of our people, Your Honors, not from the point of view of the judges,” Panganiban added.
(You may be 20, 24, two judges…what our people are asking from you is justice. They do not really dwell on who will give that justice. But for them, they want to see and feel that there is justice.)
Panganiban pushed the envelope further by calling for the inhibition of senator-judges who failed to participate in the ongoing impeachment trial proceedings.
“If I were in their position, because they are not in a position to render a truthful and fair judgment, I would even voluntarily inhibit from voting,” Panganiban said.
Before the proceedings ended, the Senate impeachment court also ordered Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte to testify before the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Duterte.

The younger Duterte was among the individuals subpoenaed to appear on September 23, including Gerardo del Rosario, director of the company registration and monitoring department of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
House prosecution panel said the Davao City mayor could speak about Gencorp Industries, Inc., a firm linked to his sister.

"Ang gusto natin malaman dito, in his capacity as mayor of Davao, kung nagkaroon ba ng dealings itong company na ito with the city government of Davao. Kung ano 'yung details? Let's see when he is called to the stand," said private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. said in a press briefing.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?
articles.summary: Following Manuel Neuer's retirement, there are many candidates to succeed him, but which goalkeeper will Jürgen Klopp choose? What factors will play a role, and will Neuer's future have an indirect…

image.caption: Many believe Jonas Urbig (right) is the natural successor to Manuel Neuer (left)Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: After Germany's early exit from the 2026 World Cup, Manuel Neuer retired from international duty, opening the door for a new number one.

Jonas Urbig appears the obvious choice, but Neuer is still number one at Bayern Munich, which severely limits Urbig's playing time. If the 23-year-old was Bayern's first choice, he would likely be Germany's number one too. As it stands, though, it appears doubtful that Germany's new coach Jürgen Klopp will even call him up to his first squad. On September 17, he will announce his squad for four UEFA Nations League games against the Netherlands, Greece, and Serbia. And no position in the current Germany team is more up for grabs than goalkeeper.
Oliver Baumann: The automatic Neuer replacement?

Oliver Baumann represents exactly that kind of selfless number two that could be the next number one. The Hoffenheim goalkeeper even commendably dealt with the humiliation of being replaced by Neuer just before the World Cup.

blocks.caption: Oliver Baumann appears unlikely to be Germany's new number one under KloppImage: Michael Memmler/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, Klopp isn’t just tasked with celebrating short-term success with Germany. His remit is to bring about lasting change, making Germany favorites for a World Cup and a Euros once again. Oliver Baumann turned 36 this summer. The Bundesliga veteran will be 38 at the next Euros, 40 by the 2030 World Cup. His age might count against a sustainable rebirth of the Germany team.

The Hoffenheim goalkeeper, who has 13 caps, spoke to Bild in the days leading up to the squad announcement about his exchange with Klopp: "Yes, I was in contact with him. He'll say everything else on Thursday. We'll see about the rest—that’s for him to handle."
Ter Stegen: Back in Germany colors via Ajax?

Since Klopp prefers a highly attacking style of play in which all players press high up the field, he might opt for a goalkeeper who can also take on the duties of a field player. Marc-André ter Stegen would fit this profile better than Baumann. Ter Stegen is also two years younger than his competitor, though his career has been hampered by injuries.

blocks.caption: Perhaps Marc-André ter Stegen will find his way back into the Germany team via Ajax?Image: Van der Velden/Fotostand/picture alliance

blocks.text: After several serious injuries and a legal dispute with Barcelona, ter Stegen has gone on loan to Ajax, improving his chances of returning between the posts for Germany.

"As far as ter Stegen is concerned, I assume he’ll definitely be in the mix," Lothar Matthäus recently wrote for Sky. "If he continues to perform well in Amsterdam, he's a candidate for the number one spot."
Alexander Nübel: Out of the spotlight in Turkey

Alexander Nübel was Germany's third-string goalkeeper at the World Cup. He had been consistent at Stuttgart but moved to Besiktas this summer, where he has made a strong start. However, former national team goalkeeper Toni Schumacher sees the move as a disadvantage for the 29-year-old.

"His move to Turkey has taken him out of the spotlight," Schumacher, who also played for Fenerbahce for three years during his playing days, told Bild. "It simply has a positive effect when you play in your own country week after week and thrill the fans with your saves."
Loris Karius: History with Klopp at Liverpool
A goalkeeper who has never been called up to the Germany team but shares a history with Jürgen Klopp is Loris Karius.

blocks.caption: Once considered one of Germany's most promising goalkeepers, Loris Karius appears to now, aged 33, have a real chance of being in the Germany set-up Image: Norbert Schmidt/picture alliance

blocks.text: Karius, who has been at Schalke since January 2025, was at times Klopp’s number one at Liverpool. However, he made two critical mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final against Real Madrid and was subsequently dropped.
Back in the Bundesliga aged 33, Karius is now delivering consistent performances and may have played his way back into the spotlight.
"When people associate me with that, it's a testament to the performance I’m putting in. That's great," Karius said recently in an interview with Sky.
Several keepers who could play for Germany or somewhere else

If none of the obvious candidates get selected, there are also a number of other good goalkeepers who might be considered. First among them is Noah Atubolu. The 24-year-old Eintracht Frankfurt keeper, who has Nigerian heritage, was the number one for Germany's U21s from 2022 to 2025, and was called up to the senior squad once last October.

blocks.caption: Finn Dahmen (left) and Noah Atubolu (right) are both young keepers with potentialImage: Sebastian Räppold/Matthias Koch/picture alliance

blocks.text: Freiburg's Mio Backhaus is another promising talent. The 22-year-old’s mother is from Japan, meaning Backhaus is also eligible to play for Japan. He even played for the Japanese U15 team, but has since progressed through Germany's youth teams up to the U21 level.
In addition to Atubolu and Backhaus, there are also Augsburg's Finn Dahmen (28), Stuttgart's Dennis Seimen (20), and Diant Ramaj (24), who left recently relegated Heidenheim to join Copenhagen.

If Klopp wants to rely on one of the five, it might be worth playing them sooner rather than later in a competitive game. After all, just like Atubolu and Backhaus, the other three are also eligible to play for another country due to their heritage. Dahmen could also play for England, Seimen for Romania, and Ramaj for Kosovo.
Köpke: 'Develop a young keeper as new number one'
"I think they need to develop a young goalkeeper as the number one right now," Andreas Köpke, the goalkeeper on Germany's 1996 European championship team, told Bild.
Germany's former goalkeeping coach pointed to Bayern's backup goalkeeper Urbig alongside Backhaus and Atubolu—though only as and when Urbig plays regulary at club level.
And given his standing at Bayern, that's bound to come down to how long Manuel Neuer choses to continue to play.

articles.title: Dispatch from the ICC grounds: A waving Duterte, tears of joy, delaying tactics
articles.summary: Just after the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III adjourned the third status conference for Rodrigo Duterte"s upcoming trial, the former president looked out and waved at viewers in…

blocks.text: THE HAGUE, Netherlands — Just after the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III adjourned the third status conference for Rodrigo Duterte’s upcoming trial, the former president looked out and waved at viewers in the public gallery.
The gesture lasted only a few seconds as the gallery curtain closed, leaving several Duterte supporters tearing up.

Unlike previous hearings in Duterte’s ICC case, only a few supporters attended today’s status conference, as they did not expect the former president to appear today. The other viewers were students touring the ICC, a handful of journalists, and other local visitors.
“Looking good”
The conference started promptly at 10:30 AM local time (4:30 PM Manila), with the gallery curtain slowly opening up.

From our position in the media seats, Duterte was on the far end of the defense side. My journalist colleagues and I had been anticipating his appearance since there was no publicized request from his counsel, Peter Haynes, to waive his attendance before the court.
As the judges entered the courtroom, Duterte was seated with his right hand on his chin – a posture reminiscent of one of his presidential portraits.

Before the prosecution began their presentation, the journalists had a good five minutes spent observing the former president – who, as the photos of the day show, sports long hair and dons a black jacket and white inner shirt – before leaving the gallery to break the news.
For some journalists, he was “looking good”, far from a mental image of an emaciated Duterte that his relatives had described some months back.

A photojournalist, whom I briefly spoke with as I left the gallery, described Duterte as “looking happy” when she saw him entering the courtroom. She said the former president “invited” them to go to “our beautiful country of the Philippines.”
“Tears of joy”
When we returned to the gallery, I saw some smiling supporters locking their gaze on the former president, while others clasped their hands, as if praying.
Janet Suliman, a long-time Duterte supporter, said she cried “tears of joy” when she saw Duterte – his first public appearance before the Court since March 14, 2025.
She and other supporters told me they had expected him to appear in a wheelchair or in a visibly worse condition.

“He’s a fighter,” Suliman said. “He looked confident. We believe he knows that he didn’t do anything wrong.” She added that they would continue to stand by Duterte “until the end” and that “justice would prevail.”
I told Suliman that the relatives of drug war victims also want that justice as well. However, she said that some killed during the drug war “fought back” against the police.

Other supporters, Cecil van Hameren, Alma Knoester, Jennifer Carcueba and Alvin Sarzate, questioned the volume of evidence the prosecution presented after Duterte’s defense said its evidence list had grown to nearly 20,000 items.
They described the number as “unbelievable” and questioned how prosecutors could have gathered and prepared such a large amount of material.
“Magician,” one supporter said, referring to the prosecution.
Others dismissed the evidence as “made up” and “nonsense.”

The prosecution has maintained that its evidence supports the charges against Duterte, while his defense team has raised separate concerns about the volume and organization of the material disclosed in the case.
Delaying tactic

The Duterte Panagutin Network (DPN) and other critics of the former president likewise anticipated his first appearance in court – but they rejected claims from his lawyers about his health and fitness to stand trial.

Although none of the DPN members watched the conference in the gallery, they told me during their protest outside the ICC grounds that they would stay tuned, considering Duterte’s appearance before the court was already a “big win” for the relatives of drug war victims who yearn to hold him accountable.

Fiona Magallanes of Bayan Netherlands and convenor of Panagutin Network Netherlands wrote in a statement that Duterte’s health arguments were his camp’s “delaying tactic”. She said the group hopes to see him appear again when his trial starts, which has been scheduled on November 30.
"Duterte's appearance in court today proves he has been feigning sick all this time. It was all a delaying tactic, delaying justice and delaying healing for the victims’ families,” she said.
Magallanes also said Duterte “looks well,” which she claimed was “exposing the myth that his camp has continuously pushed of a sickly old man supposedly ‘unfit to stand trial.’”

Duterte’s lawyers have argued before the ICC that he suffers from cognitive impairment affecting his memory and ability to participate meaningfully in the proceedings. The Trial Chamber has yet to rule on his fitness to stand trial.
Planned demonstrations

The next status conference, based on the ICC court calendar, is scheduled for October 13. Duterte’s supporters told me they are gearing up for protests leading up to the November 30 trial. The Netherlands-based Duterte Panagutin Network, meanwhile, has already scheduled demonstrations on the first day of the trial. — BAP, GMA News
