articles.title: Belarus to release 25 more prisoners as US eases sanctions
articles.summary: Belarus will release 25 more prisoners under an interim agreement with the United States, while Washington plans to lift sanctions on two Belarusian companies and pursue broader negotiations.

image.caption: Several prisoners from Belarus were also freed earlier this yearImage: BNS/IMAGO

blocks.text: Belarus will release 25 prisoners in exchange for a further easing of US sanctions, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.

"We agreed on an interim agreement, and as a show of goodwill, Belarus will release 25 people. In exchange, the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," envoy John Coale told reporters in the Belarusian capital, Minsk.

Coale had reportedly requested the release of 250 prisoners during his visit last March. The US special envoy said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues and secure the release of additional prisoners as well as the removal of further sanctions.
"We will continue to improve relations between the United States and Belarus and are working to secure the release of more people in the near future. We are not done!" he later posted on X.

Hundreds of people remain in prison in Belarus after President Alexander Lukashenko carried out a crackdown on protests against his reelection in 2020. Western countries then slapped sanctions on the country as a result of Lukashenko's repression of opposition.
Accusations against Lukashenko

Human rights organization Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the government still holds more than 900 political prisoners. The detainees have been accused of extremism, conspiracy to seize power, incitement of hatred, or insulting the president.

blocks.caption: Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales ​Bialiatski was released from Belarusian prison in late 2025 as part of a US-brokered dealImage: Petras Malukas/AFP

blocks.text: During Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the existence of political prisoners and rejected Viasna's claims.

The two companies to be removed from the US sanctions list are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of industrial paints and coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned company that oversees the forestry, pulp, and paper sectors. These sanctions have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also announced the release of tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets currently held in US banks.

articles.title: SC welcomes fair criticism amid VP Sara's distrust of justice system
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) responded to Vice President Sara Duterte"s remarks expressing distrust of the justice system, saying that it welcomed fair criticisms but needed evidence to act on.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 7:59pm

Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court-Branch 98 on Saturday, September 5, 2026, a day after it ordered her arrest for her grave threats case. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez
The Supreme Court (SC) responded to Vice President Sara Duterte’s remarks expressing distrust of the justice system, saying that it welcomed fair criticisms but needed evidence to act on.
In a 24 Oras report on Wednesday, SC spokesperson Camille Ting said that the decision-making of the courts was based on evidence.

“In my previous statement issued lately, we said naman the Court invites fair criticism as long as it’s… I mean we shouldn’t be very sensitive about the criticisms from the public, but then any action from the court will need evidence,” Ting said.

Duterte aired her frustration about the country’s justice system when sheposted bail at the Quezon City Hall of Justice for her three counts of grave threats against President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.
“I do not feel safe, I really do not feel safe. I don’t trust the court, I don’t trust the police,” Duterte told her lawyers and surrounding reporters.
Duterte posted bail of P360,000 and was able to walk free afterwards. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Congo's Ebola epidemic may have gone undetected for months
articles.summary: The deadliest Ebola outbreak on record in the Democratic Republic of Congo may have begun months before it was first declared in May.

image.caption: As of September 12, Congolese authorities had recorded 7,200 cases in seven provinces with 3,475 deathsImage: Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Democratic Republic of Congo officially declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo variant on May 15. However, the first infections likely occurred much earlier.

Just how far back the start of the epidemic actually goes is still a matter of debate. But one thing is certain: Congolese authorities did not respond in the best possible way, with several international organizations highlighting delays in the initial response.
Congo is no stranger to crisis response. The country experiences Ebola outbreaks on a regular basis, and has in the past been praised for its expertise in combating the disease.
Early warnings came from WHO, Africa CDC

A good starting point for tracing the origins of the outbreak is the timeline provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) in collaboration with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak

According to their data, the first known case, identified retrospectively, was a health worker from Mongbwalu in northeastern Ituri Province. The person, sources said, developed symptoms characteristic of Ebola around April 24 or 25.
They died at a medical center in Bunia, the capital of Ituri. To date, 80% of all cases have been reported in the province.
It wasn't until May 5 that the WHO said it had been informed of "an unknown illness with high mortality reported in Mongbwalu Health Zone." The global health body then issued its first warning.
Congo's delayed response questioned as Ebola spread
Ten days later, on May 15, the Congolese government announced the Ebola outbreak.
Tests conducted by the National Institute for Biomedical Research in Kinshasa had confirmed the presence of the rare Bundibugyo type of Ebola.
Three days later, the Africa CDC raised concerns about the speed of Congo's response.
About three weeks had passed between the onset of the first symptoms in the suspected index case and the laboratory confirmation — even though the fatality was a health worker.

"This significant delay [...] highlights a critically low initial index of clinical suspicion among local healthcare providers, which facilitated wider geographic spread prior to the initiation of containment efforts," the Africa CDC concluded.
According to reports gathered by DW, residents of Mongbwalu had already reported suspicious deaths as early as the end of April.

"Several deaths were reported following high fevers, and the victims often showed traces of blood around various body orifices," said Dieudonne Lossa Dekhana, the provincial coordinator for civil society in Ituri.
Red Cross reported 'widespread' public fear 'since March 30'
There were other indications that Ebola was already circulating long before the emergence of this first confirmed case.

A May 16 report by the Red Cross of the Democratic Republic of the Congo stated: "Since March 30, 2026, there has been widespread fear among the population of the Mongbwalu Health Zone following a series of deaths."
Here, too, the symptoms matched those of Ebola: high fever, chest pain, severe exhaustion, persistent cough, nosebleeds, vomiting, loss of consciousness, a comatose state and ultimately death.

The Red Cross report said the trigger was believed to have been the body of a Mongbwalu resident "who died and was placed in a coffin purchased in Bunia, which was then replaced by another in Mongbwalu."
DR Congo: Ebola survivors fight misinformation
US researchers: February outbreak is plausible

The funeral that brought various people into direct contact with the body and the contaminated coffin is believed to have been the cause of a rising number of infections and deaths that were subsequently observed in Mongbwalu and Bunia.

But from the data available, it is not possible to confirm without doubt that these deaths were related to the Bundibugyo virus. However, they show that an unusual health phenomenon had already been observed more than six weeks before the outbreak was officially declared on May 15.
In addition, investigations since May 15 have come to support the thesis that Ebola might have been circulating even earlier than that.

In a study published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on June 11, a team of researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reconstructed the early course of the epidemic.

An initial transmission from an animal to a human, or spillover, between mid- and late February is "plausible," the researchers concluded. A late-April spillover, on the other hand, would be difficult to reconcile with the scale the epidemic had already reached at the time of the study.
WHO: Genome sequencing suggests February outbreak
On August 10, Mohamed Janabi, the WHO Regional Director for Africa, said genome sequencing analyses suggested the outbreak likely began "as early as February 2026."
Several early infections were mistakenly attributed to diseases that were far more common in the region, particularly malaria and typhus, he said.

In an August interview, Janabi told DW that there was a significant gap in case reporting. "The Ebola situation is catastrophic... In three months, we only had access to one-third of the patients," he said.

blocks.caption: Efforts to contain the virus have increased as the caseload risesImage: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/REUTERS

blocks.text: Could 'pig Ebola' shed some light on the matter?
Jules Villa, a researcher in the anthropology and ecology of disease emergence at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, points to a phenomenon observed in the connection with previous Ebola epidemics.
Villa'sstudy does not encompass the 2026 outbreak, but takes stock of local reports collected during earlier Ebola outbreaks in northeastern Congo.
Villa shows that livestock farmers, veterinarians and residents had reported unusually high animal mortality even before the outbreak of at least two Ebola epidemics in humans.
In 2017, several witnesses reported on what they called "pig Ebola" — a high mortality among pigs, which was ultimately attributed to swine fever.
According to Villa's research, monitoring livestock in the general population could provide the first useful warning signs long before an outbreak is confirmed by a laboratory.
Why is Trump investing $242 million in DRC Ebola response?
This article was originally written in French.

articles.title: Duterte team hits Prosecution's disclosure; prosec says defense is exaggerating
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team on Wednesday slammed the Prosecution"s disclosure of its evidence in the former official"s crimes against humanity case, saying that it is in a…

blocks.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team on Wednesday slammed the Prosecution’s disclosure of its evidence in the former official’s crimes against humanity case, saying that it is in a “terrible mess.”

During the third status conference before the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III, Duterte’s counsel, Peter Haynes, said that there are around 62,000 exhibits “dumped” in the Registry.

“Mr. Nicholls, I think unintentionally, has kind of muddied the waters here. Because the large disclosure package he referred to is not within that 19,000… nearly 20,000. That’s additional to that,” he said.

“And what has been dumped in the Registry is 62,500 exhibits. That 324,000 pages of evidence and over 1,000 video and audio files which run to many thousands of hours. And they’re in a terrible mess,” he added.
Haynes said evidence has been in the possession of the Prosecution since November 2021.
“That’s nearly five years. And the first time we knew about the large tranche was the 15th of July, six weeks before the end of disclosure,” he said.
According to Haynes, they looked into the possibility of acquiring an AI tool to review the documents.
However, he said it would cost nearly €500,000.
Haynes also argued that it was not their job to inspect the material.
“They’re supposed to triage this material and disclose it having read it. They’ve never read it. And they’ve had it for five years,” he said.

“As I say, I’m not going to go into the correspondence, but I have in front of me an email where we say, explicitly, we are not going to assume responsibility for inspecting and assessing the relevance of the documents in your possession,” he added.
Meanwhile, Haynes informed the Court that some documents were disclosed page by page.
He said a partial solution is a “meta data update,” but added that this only establishes the connection point between the pages.
“It doesn’t put them together in one document. There are still 400 separate exhibits,” he said.
Exaggeration
For his part, Prosecutor and Senior Trial Lawyer Julian Nicholls said that what Haynes said was not entirely accurate and was “really exaggerated, in [his] view.”
“Yes, there may be some duplicates… I’m not saying it’s perfect, but that was not an accurate picture.
In response, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said that the example presented by Haynes did not “inspire them with much confidence.”
Earlier, Nicholls also said that he and the defense have yet to agree on facts.

“So far, the agreement on agreed facts has been exactly zero. At this moment, we have to prove that he was mayor of Davao. At this moment, we have to prove he was elected president and that he served as president,” he said.
Korner told the Prosecution to produce a list of key items of evidence.
Meanwhile, she directed the defense to submit into writing its complaints or suggestions within seven days.
She also gave the Prosecution seven days to give its reply.
Korner also advised the parties to discuss with each other.
Duterte, who is is facing charges over alleged killings during his time as President and Davao City mayor, attended his status conference for the first time.
He sat behind his defense team.
In the few moments that the former official was shown in the livestream, he appeared to be listening intently. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte defense considered AI amid massive ICC evidence review
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte's defense team said it considered using artificial intelligence (AI) and other electronic methods to review tens of thousands of documents related to his case, but…
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 7:11pm

THE HAGUE, Netherlands — Former president Rodrigo Duterte's defense team said it considered using artificial intelligence (AI) and other electronic methods to review tens of thousands of documents related to his case, but found that a suitable AI tool could cost nearly half a million euros (almost P36.18 million).

The issue came up during Wednesday's status conference before the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III as Duterte's counsel Peter Haynes raised concerns over the volume and organization of evidence disclosed by the prosecution.
Duterte appeared in person before the Court for the first time since his initial appearance hearing in March 2025.
Haynes said the prosecution's evidence list contains nearly 20,000 items, compared to about 5,000 at the confirmation stage.

"We haven't got a prayer of reading 20,000 items of evidence by a trial date that starts at the end of November, and even less a prayer of dealing with them in our brief, which has to be filed on the 30th of October," Haynes said.
He also told the Chamber that a separate disclosure package involved 62,500 items, around 324,000 pages of evidence and more than 1,000 audio and video files.
Trial Chamber III presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked whether the fact that the records are now digital and searchable could allow the defense to review them more quickly through electronic methods.

"Because it's all digitalized, it's more searchable. And provided you give it terms that meet the criteria, it is possible to go through it quicker than we're all in the proverbial boxes in a warehouse," the judge said.
Haynes said the defense had already researched the possibility of using AI.
"We did research the possibility of acquiring an AI tool to do it, and it will cost very nearly half a million euros," he said.

The defense also argued that prosecutors should have reviewed and sorted the materials before it was disclosed. Haynes said part of the material had been in the prosecution's possession since November 2021.
"They're supposed to triage this material and disclose it, having read it. They've never read it, and they've had it for five years," Haynes said.

Haynes described several problems with the disclosure, including individual pages of the same document being filed separately and assigned different evidence numbers. He said one 400-page document had been disclosed page by page, with the defense receiving 347 of the 400 pages.
He proposed moving a smaller set of materials to a new case file and limiting the disclosure there to around 10,000 documents.
'Really exaggerated'

The prosecution disputed Haynes' description of the disclosure. ICC Senior Trial Lawyer Julian Nicholls said the defense's account was "not all accurate" and "really exaggerated," although he acknowledged that some duplicates and other problems may exist.
The Chamber said the issue should be resolved quickly and ordered the defense to put its concerns and proposed solution in writing.
"So, Mr. Haynes, we'll give you seven days. We'll say close business by next Wednesday to file a motion about this," the judge said.
The prosecution will then be given seven days to respond.
The judge also urged both sides to try to settle the disclosure issues between themselves, while acknowledging the difficulties involved "even with electronic methods."
"We obviously have to resolve this sooner rather than later," the judge said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Legendary Nigerian actor Olu Jacobs dies aged 84
articles.summary: Olu Jacobs was one of Nigeria's most recognised actors, whose career spanned several decades.

blocks.text: Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.
His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.
Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".
Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.
He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.
"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.

Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.
He later became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.
His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.
In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.

Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.
In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

articles.title: Duterte makes first appearance before ICC judges
articles.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the ICC as judges considered claims of memory impairment and poor health. The 81-year-old is accused of crimes against humanity.

image.caption: Lawyers for the 81-year-old have said he is suffering from cognitive declineImage: International Criminal Court/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines, made his first in-person appearance before judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) at a pretrial hearing on Wednesday.
The 81-year-old faces charges of crimes against humanity in connection with hundreds of murders committed during his "war on drugs" while in office.
Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, denies the allegations.
He has missed a series of hearings since he was arrested in March 2025 and has previously appeared in court via videolink.
Duterte's legal team have said he suffers from poor health, but the court's judges ruled in January that he was fit enough to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court.
The ex-president "suffers from a significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing his memories," his lawyers said.
The prosecution, meanwhile, argued Duterte was "capable of meaningfully exercising his procedural and fair trial rights, and that he is fit for trial."
Philippines: Duterte 'must face reckoning' for drug war
What is Duterte accused of?
Rodrigo Duterte is accused of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, first when he was the mayor of the southern city of Davao and then as Philippine president.
Prosecutors say he is responsible for a systematic campaign that led to the deaths of at least 30,000 people, many of them during "anti-drug" raids.
Duterte's trial is scheduled for November this year.
During Wednesday's pretrial hearing, judges were to hear arguments about his health and decide whether he is mentally fit to stand trial.

articles.title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says
articles.summary: The two countries accounted for 52% of killings of environmental activists in 2025, according to Global Witness.

blocks.text: Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness, external.
Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26.
Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012.
Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states.
Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years.
Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says.
Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed.
Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining.
Last week, Jacob Guachetá Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed.

While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory.
Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024.
As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found.
Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders.
The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported.

articles.title: [OPINION] Expanding armies, shrinking peace: Militarization in Southeast Asia
articles.summary: These examples of military-led approaches in the region may each temporarily contain dissent, but likely also exacerbate human suffering while failing to reduce either armed or non-armed opposition

blocks.text: Several nations in Southeast Asia have undergone military expansion and increased securitization over the past decade contributing to what many observers describe as a regional arms race.

The ongoing militarization in Southeast Asia, combined with the erosion of the liberal international order and the weakening of democratic and human rights norms, has contributed to a self-reinforcing cycle of violence involving state militaries and domestic armed oppositions.

Rather than addressing the political causes of conflict, military solutions prolong insecurity, intensify armed confrontation, and exacerbate human suffering in conflict-affected communities such as Myanmar, the Philippines and Indonesia.

After the illegal 2021 military coup overthrew the elected government, military authorities intensified their repression of political expression, launched large-scale counteroffensive operations against armed resistance groups, expanded conscription, and gradually increased both conventional and unconventional aerial attacks on civilian and military targets.

An estimated 90% of Myanmar’s population has been exposed to conflict. Over 3.5 million people have been displaced, while one in three citizens now require humanitarian assistance. The scale of insecurity has transformed Myanmar into one of the world’s most severe humanitarian and protection crises.

The Myanmar military, which is responsible for the vast majority of political violence in the country, has demonstrated little genuine commitment to resolving the political crisis fueling nationwide conflict. Airstrikes and attacks against civilian populations continue despite junta leader Min Aung Hlaing’s 100-day peace plan, killing over 600 between April 20 to July 31.

For the junta, peace talks appear to be less aimed at achieving conflict resolution than at managing threats to its authority and fragmenting opposition coalitions. Dialogue risks becoming a mechanism where the military prioritises regime survival over the pursuit of durable and inclusive peace. Recent China-brokered ceasefires between the military and Ethnic Armed Organisations operating in northern Shan state reflect the military’s longstanding divide-and-rule strategy: neutralising one adversary through ceasefire agreements while intensifying military operations against others.

The Myanmar military faces limited external pressure to change while it is backed by international partners such as China and Russia, which continue to provide it with military equipment and technical assistance, and the junta also benefits from varying degrees of diplomatic engagement from neighboring countries such as India and Thailand.
The New People’s Army (NPA), widely regarded as Asia’s longest-running communist insurgency, has been engaged in armed conflict with successive Philippines governments since 1968.

Since President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared in July 2024 that the rebellion had effectively ceased, armed confrontations between state forces and insurgents have continued and, in some areas, intensified. April 2026 marked the deadliest month for the insurgency in recent years, with counterinsurgency operations reportedly resulting in 19 deaths, including six civilians. Overall, at least 390 combatants and civilians were reportedly killed in insurgency-related and counterinsurgency violence in 2025 alone.

Separately, Manila has deepened defence and security cooperation with the US and other regional partners amid growing tensions in the South China Sea. Joint military exercises, technology transfers, expanded access to military facilities, and new defence agreements have been justified by the Marcos administration as necessary measures to strengthen deterrence and protect Philippine sovereignty. However, these developments may also contribute to the militarization of areas where insurgent activity persists, including parts of Luzon, potentially complicating local conflict dynamics.
Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto is pushing to project power outside Southeast Asia.

He seeks to transform Indonesia into one of the world’s 10 largest developed economies by 2045 while simultaneously improving military capabilities. Indonesia has also sought to strengthen its international profile by joining US President Donald Trump’s controversial Board of Peace platform. Through these initiatives, Jakarta aims to present itself as a responsible actor committed to international peace and security, supported by a strong defence posture.

Domestically, the administration led by Prabowo Subianto, a former military general, regularly faces strident public opposition to its economic and populist policies and armed resistance in the province of Papua. Prabowo’s flagship “free lunch” program, which many Papuans perceived as facilitating greater military presence and settlement by military families in the region, generated significant opposition. The Indonesian government has deployed thousands of Indonesian Armed Forces and police to Papua since January 2025.

blocks.caption: Indonesian government puts out full page newspaper ad on military’s expanded role

blocks.text: One consequence of the increased security presence in Papua, has been a rise in military operations. According to conflict monitors, state forces have carried out 78 air and drone strikes since Prabowo assumed the presidency in October 2024. A military operation in April 2026 extended beyond active combat zones and struck civilian areas, including a refugee sanctuary previously recognised by both the Indonesian military and the West Papua National Liberation Army in Kambru District, blurring the distinction between combatants and non-combatants. The resulting security deterioration has produced a severe humanitarian crisis, with more than 100,000 people reportedly displaced across Papua as of March 2026.

At the international level, military cooperation and defense ties with foreign governments provide the Indonesian military with access to weapons, training, and logistical support, enabling the continuation of counterinsurgency operations in Papua.
These examples of military-led approaches in the region may each temporarily contain dissent, but likely also exacerbate human suffering while failing to reduce either armed or non-armed opposition.

Achieving peace requires a fundamentally different approach: prioritising peaceful conflict resolution over military responses, recognising historical injustices, facilitating meaningful dialogue between states and affected communities, providing impartial mediation, addressing long-standing grievances, ensuring accountability and the right to truth, creating conditions for reconciliation, supporting inclusive socio-economic development, and establishing political systems that accommodate diverse interests.

Without at least some of this work, genuine peace will remain out of reach. The relatively successful peace processes in the region, such as those in Aceh, Indonesia, and the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in the Philippines demonstrate that durable peace requires sustained peace-building efforts even long after formal agreements are reached. – Rappler.com

Su Mon has provided the following: Su Mon is ACLED’s Regional Expert and the 2025 Conflict and Peace Research Fellow at the Australian National University and University of Melbourne. (ACLED is Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Asia Pacific).

articles.title: 'We will rule in CANADA': Letter from Bishnoi gang to police disclosed to CBC News
articles.summary: CBC News has obtained a copy of a letter sent from the Lawrence Bishnoi gang to Canada's "defence minister, army and police" claiming to have 5,000 gang members in Canada and "more guns" than the…

image.caption: Bishnoi gang member Arshdeep Singh had this image on his Facebook profile, which was captured by police as part of an investigation into a gang linked to extortion, shootings, arson and vehicle fraud in multiple provinces. (CBC News)

blocks.text: CBC News has obtained a copy of a letter the Lawrence Bishnoi gang sent Canada's "defence minister, army and police" last year claiming to have 5,000 gang members in Canada and "more guns" than the police.

The letter sent to the Abbotsford Police Department and signed "Lawrence gang from India" was released through an Access to Information Act request for exhibits from an Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) hearing for a Bishnoi associate who was ordered deported in July.
A police officer who testified at the hearing referred to the letter's existence, but the full text has never been made public.

"We are giving you a written warning and challenge. We are Indian gang Canada has no guts to stop us is that clear — we will rule in CANADA now no one can stop us we are very powerful," reads the letter, which is riddled with spelling errors and lacks punctuation.
"This is our time now Indian we have more than 5000 gang member in Canada they can do shooting for only $1000 can you stop us no way. You will see we will takeover CANADA soon."
'Tactical Guide' to the Bishnoi gang

The letter is part of a trove of documents and videos highlighting multi-jurisdictional, multi-agency efforts to disrupt the amorphous cells of young Indian nationals behind the extortion crisis gripping Canadian communities.
The documents include allegations against two men identified by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) this week for their links to Bishnoi-related extortion cases.

According to the files, Amitoz Bajwa and Sahibjot Singh were part of a web of Edmonton-based suspects in their early 20s implicated in shootings and threats against victims in Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia.
The documents include the CBSA's "Tactical Guide" to the Bishnoi organization, which traces the gang's growth in Canada from 2023 to late 2025.

items: Inside an extortion deportation case: The arsons, auto frauds and shootings linking crime across Canada

blocks.text: Lawrence Bishnoi has been in jail in India since 2015, but has built an international organization from behind bars.
In Canada, Bishnoi has allegedly relied on his top lieutenant, Goldy Brar, who obtained a student permit in 2017 to attend Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops.
It's unknown if Brar actually attended classes, but he filed a refugee claim in 2019 which was deemed abandoned in 2022. His current whereabouts are unknown.

items: 'Danger to the public': The story behind the deportation of a 'Ruffian'

blocks.text: Goldy Brar and Goldy Dhillon
According to the documents, Brar and Lawrence Bishnoi split last year, becoming rivals.

"It is unclear if Goldy is leveraging his split from the Bishnoi Gang to take over operations in Canada, as recent intelligence indicates that Goldy's name is the one most often used in extortion cases in [Alberta]," the CBSA's guide reads.

This summer, the FBI posted a $50,000 reward for information leading to Brar's capture after announcing charges against Bishnoi and his associates for conspiracy and killings including the alleged murder of Sikh separatist leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey in 2023.

The CBSA's tactical guide names other gang leaders behind extortion cases in Canada, including Goldy Dhillon, a subcontractor believed responsible for "recruiting 'foot soldiers' to carry out criminal activities including targeted attacks and extortions in India and Canada."

Both Dhillon and Brar's names feature prominently in one of the most revealing documents contained in the information released to CBC News: a detailed ongoing investigative summary compiled by the Organized Crime Branch of the Edmonton Police Service.
'They all have to pay us'

At nearly 200 pages, the report on the probe known as Project Garter reads like a police procedural novel, with a through-line drawn from the daily reports of investigators overseeing more than a dozen files involving multiple extortion victims.
The investigation covers seven months starting in May 2025. The letter from the Bishnoi gang was delivered in mid-August 2025 and is copied verbatim into the report.
"Very soon every business owner have to pay protection money to us it is like TAX," the letter reads.
"No other way around for any business. so do not try to stop us and doesn't matter Indian or white or black community businessman they all have to pay us."
The report claims the letter fits a pattern of threats from the "Lawrence Group" and "the Lawrence Bishnoi Group" attached to shootings and extortion cases across the country.

In the Project Garter files, ballistics reports linked shootings in Edmonton, Calgary and Surrey. Police also doggedly followed social media accounts of suspects and obtained search warrants and tracking warrants for vehicles and phones to pinpoint movement.

When a Ford Mustang was reportedly stolen and used for drive-by shootings, investigators grilled one of the owners who reported the theft of the vehicle, combing through Instagram and the vehicle's "infotainment system" data to link the owner to other gang members.
'I am talking from Lawrence Bishnoi group'
The report also describes multiple victims, including the owner of a giant business targeted for millions of dollars by a suspect who verbally identified himself as Goldy Dhillon.
The victim told police another family member had also seen his Surrey-based business burned to the ground after similar demands.
Jashandeep Singh holding a gun
In a separate incident, police warned another man about credible threats to his life.

The demands for money came from more than a dozen WhatsApp numbers — at least two of which were also linked to extortion files investigated by Peel Regional Police in Ontario. The report includes the translated text of one message left after a victim refused to respond.

"I am talking from Lawrence Bishnoi group. This time I shot at your house, next time it’s going to be you. I know exactly what your system is. Where you are what you do, I can find you," the message reads.
“Either talk to us and settle this and it will be good for you guys. Or shots will be fired at your entire family. Not answering the phone will not make this go away."
A gun with a pink slide

The documents obtained by CBC News were compiled by the CBSA for disclosure at an IRB hearing that resulted in a ruling of inadmissibility for Jashandeep Singh — a 25-year-old who came to Canada as a student in December 2022.

Singh was tied to the group through his friendship with Arshdeep Singh, a mid-level Bishnoi leader deported from Canada earlier this year after he was also found inadmissible for organized criminality.
Jashandeep Singh was accused of helping to conceal a distinctive weapon that linked Arshdeep Singh to shootings in Surrey and Edmonton.
The documents presented at the IRB included a video of Jashandeep Singh pointing the gun — which has a pink slide — to a friend's head.
Arshdeep Singh holding a gun

CBC News has previously reported on the broad scope of allegations against Arshdeep Singh, but the police report includes detailed information about his alleged activities and an analysis of the contents of his phone.
Phone intercepts caught Arshdeep Singh talking about trafficking in heroin, opioids and cocaine and bragging about committing a murder that happened when he would have been 12 years old.
He was also allegedly caught speaking to an associate about shooting incidents in Surrey and instructing them to "go to your city and gather some weapons."

items: 'I didn't know': Alleged member of extortion gang claims he had no idea friend connected to shootings

blocks.text: According to the documents, Arshdeep Singh has been linked to extortion cases in Ontario, including one in which he was caught on video allegedly directing others to throw Molotov cocktails at a building.

An analysis of his phone included messages containing information about dozens of vehicles which were later reported stolen — uncovering a ring in which thieves worked with owners to target cars and trucks, altering identifying information and defrauding insurance companies.
But it was the gun with the pink slide that would prove Arshdeep Singh's undoing.
According to testimony from Jashandeep Singh's IRB hearing, Arshdeep Singh came to Edmonton in August 2025 from Calgary to celebrate his birthday.

The evidence disclosed to the IRB includes videos of Arshdeep Singh and others fooling around with the gun at Jashandeep Singh's residence, before driving to a remote highway location with the weapon for further celebration.
Arshdeep Singh driving next to a gun
Arshdeep Singh can then be seen in a video firing the weapon into the air at least five times. A birthday cake sits on the trunk of his car as his friends watch.

According to the police report, investigators saw the video on social media and attended the scene after Arshdeep Singh and the others left, finding bullet casings which ballistics reports would later match to one in a string of shootings at Kap's Cafe in Surrey.

That discovery set in motion a chain of police activity resulting in multiple arrests, the execution of numerous search warrants, the discovery of more weapons and, ultimately, the gathering of evidence that would result in deportation orders against numerous suspects.

Like many of those suspected in the extortion cases, Arshdeep Singh was never convicted of a crime in Canada. But the bar for immigration inadmissibility is lower than the level of evidence needed for a criminal conviction and a person can't be deported with charges unresolved.
Arshdeep Singh didn't challenge the deportation order against him, but told his hearing he was "not involved in any of the extortion, arson, any fraud anywhere."

The final pages of the package of documents released to CBC News include worrying claims about the evolution of the extortion crisis provided to the Edmonton Police Service by a confidential informant in May 2025.

items: 'No amount of money' sufficient to stem risk of alleged Bishnoi gang member's release: lawyer
Minister of Public Safety fights to keep accused murderer and alleged Bishnoi gangster in custody

blocks.text: The informant claimed to have personal knowledge and claimed Arshdeep Singh was working for Goldy Brar, who was in turn directing people in Canada to commit extortions.
"Kidnapping people is a new extortion tactic directed by Goldy Brar. People are extorted up to $100,000.00 for a kidnapping," the informant claimed, according to a written statement.
"Young Canadian visa holders are directed to do the kidnapping."

articles.title: House suffrage chair Adiong on political dynasty bill: We intend to finish the work
articles.summary: Congress will do its duty to approve an Anti-Political Dynasty Law, Suffrage panel Chair Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said after the Supreme Court ruled that Congress must already pass the law.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 6:58pm

Congress will do its duty to approve an Anti-Political Dynasty Law, House Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms Chair Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said on Wednesday after the Supreme Court ruled that Congress must already pass the law.

"The Supreme Court has spoken on the duty. Congress must now speak through legislation. Public office is a public trust, not a hereditary entitlement. We intend to finish the work," Adiong said in a statement today.

"I welcome the Supreme Court’s reminder that Congress must enact an anti-political dynasty law defining what a political dynasty is and providing the specific prohibitions at the earliest possible time," he added.

The representative from the first district of Lanao del Sur tagged as a "constitutional wake-up call" the Supreme Court's ruling that Congress’ prolonged failure to enact an anti-political dynasty law "constitutes grave abuse of discretion.”

"For nearly four decades, Article II, Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution has directed the State to guarantee equal access to public service and prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law. The duty to define and prohibit belongs to Congress. Inaction is no longer defensible," Adiong stated.
The House of Representatives approved in June 2026 the Anti-Political Dynasty Bill on third and final reading.

The said bill prohibits relatives within the second degree of affinity and consanguinity from running simultaneously or holding elective positions in the same national, provincial, city, municipal, or barangay government, or from seeking seats in the House of Representatives within the same legislative district.
"That vote shows the House is prepared to meet the constitutional mandate identified by the Court," Alonto Adiong said.

"As Chairperson of the Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms, I reaffirm our readiness for the bicameral conference. We will work to reconcile the disagreeing provisions of the House and Senate versions so that the country finally has a clear definition, specific prohibitions, and an enforceable law," he added.

ML Party-list Rep Leila de Lima on Anti Pol Dynasty Bill: Further delaying the passage of a genuine anti-dynasty law, or enacting a law that legitimizes political dynasties, would make this abuse even graver – an injustice to the Filipino people. @gmanews @gmanewsbreaking pic.twitter.com/83TzZN4cNs— Tina PanganibanPerez (@tinapperez) September 16, 2026

In a separate statement, ML Party-list Representative Leila de Lima today expressed hope that the Senate will pass a version of the Anti Political Dynasty Law "that truly democratizes access to public office by prohibiting political dynasties, rather than giving them more license to dominate our country."
De Lima, who had authored a bill banning political dynasties, withdrew her support for the version approved by the House of Representatives.

"The Supreme Court, in its ruling granting the petitions seeking to compel Congress to pass a law on political dynasties, stated: “Congress’ failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion.” Further delaying the passage of a genuine anti-dynasty law, or enacting a law that legitimizes political dynasties, would make this abuse even graver—an injustice to the Filipino people," de Lima said in a statement.

"Kaya hindi natin naatim na suportahan ang ipinasang bersiyon ng Kamara [This is why we could not accept the version Congress passed]. After almost four decades of waiting, Filipinos are confronted with a measure that mandates the exact opposite of what the Constitution demands," she added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: US to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discrimination
articles.summary:
Announcement of visa restrictions follows Trump’s false claims of ‘white genocide’ taking place in South Africa

The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald…

blocks.text: The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners.

The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies.

Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution.

“The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X.

“The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.”

The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio said the restrictions would target those who ‘enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation’. Photograph: Saul Loeb/Reuters

blocks.text: The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activist Leo Brent Bozell III, said on X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.”
Spokespeople for South Africa’s presidency and foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Afrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.

Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute.
These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according to a 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal.
Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted.

Rubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land.

Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chant was played by Trump when he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year.
The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and therefore not hate speech.

articles.title: Chancellor Merz appeals to CDU members as AfD encroaches
articles.summary: Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, many are expressing doubts about the party's leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. But the CDU doesn't appear to have a viable…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has seen his support wane in recent monthsImage: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers (about 1,100 miles) north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various countries had gathered there for the European Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change.
When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent.

"That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said.

Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
Why is Merz so unpopular?

Another heavy defeat looks likely in the state election coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low 7%. Failure to clear the 5% hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election.

The election earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt was won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, in this central German state.

Before taking office, Merz promised he would cut support for the AfD "in half." Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system?
German Chancellor Merz reels as far-right AfD makes gains

Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change."

One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy."
When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm.

"You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now," said SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese on the Welt TV channel. "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better."

blocks.caption: Henrik Wüst (center) is often named as a possible successor to Friedrich Merz Image: Revierfoto/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst
But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor.
SU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party.

Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag.

However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment.

Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the chancellor."

Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."

blocks.caption: Markus Söder (left) has long been rumored to have ambitions for the German chancellorshipImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The statement was signed by all eight premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Pivotal state elections coming up
So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down.

If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him.

Merz's schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources have confirmed.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: At least 16 killed after building in Gaza City damaged by Israeli strikes collapses
articles.summary:
Rescue workers say search for dozens of people hampered by lack of heavy machinery

A building housing displaced Palestinian families collapsed on Wednesday in Gaza City, killing at least 16…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem, Seham Tantesh in Gaza and agencies

blocks.text: A building housing displaced Palestinian families collapsed on Wednesday in Gaza City, killing at least 16 people, as rescuers searched the rubble for dozens of people including children believed to be trapped.

A rescue team from Gaza’s civil defence said they had recovered the bodies of five children among the victims, while 14 injured people were taken to hospital. Medical sources said rescuers could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the rubble as they tried to reach them.

The bombed-out multi storey building, which contained four apartments on each floor, had previously been hit by Israeli strikes during the war, leaving its structure badly weakened and at risk of collapse. When it gave way, it fell on to tents housing displaced families beside it, witnesses said.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers remove the body of a victim from the collapsed building in south-western Gaza City. Photograph: Hamza Z H Qraiqea/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The collapse highlights the continuing danger facing tens of thousands of Palestinians living in an estimated 2,000 buildings damaged by Israeli airstrikes across Gaza.

Mohammed Abu Dan, a superviser with the civil defence team recovering victims, said more than 10 families had been living in the building and displaced people had been forced to stay there because no other shelter was available.
“Search and rescue operations are being carried out under extremely difficult conditions due to a lack of the necessary equipment and resources,” Abu Dan said.

Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israeli restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery in the territory. Israel says its restrictions are intended to prevent equipment from reaching militant groups.

A video obtained by Reuters showed rescue workers trying to pull two people from beneath a collapsed wall. Another video circulating on social media showed Gaza’s civil defence spokesperson, Mahmoud Basal, carrying a young girl wrapped in a bloodstained scarf.
Raed al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City’s civil defence service, said: “We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people.”

Alessandro Mrakic, the head of the UN Development Programme’s Gaza office, said rescuers from UN agencies were taking part in the operation, which he described as extremely difficult because of the lack of appropriate machinery. Egypt’s relief agency was also involved.
“There are actually people that are digging with their bare hands. We need to prepare [for more deaths],” Mrakic said.
Tents belonging to displaced families had been erected along the road beside the building because there was nowhere else for them to shelter.

blocks.caption: The search for survivors and the dead in the rubble continued on Wednesday. Photograph: Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Similar incidents have occurred repeatedly over the past two years, with dozens of homes and buildings damaged during the war later collapsing, trapping people and causing further deaths and injuries.

With few other options, many Palestinians have returned to partly destroyed homes or moved into abandoned buildings, clearing small spaces among the rubble despite the danger. Soaring rents and the cost of vacant land have made finding safer accommodation increasingly difficult.

Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians also remain unable to return to neighbourhoods near the so-called yellow line, forcing families to find whatever space they can elsewhere. In May, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, ordered the military to seize 70% of Gaza.

Damaged roofs, walls and supporting columns can collapse without warning, particularly during strong winds, heavy rain or further bombardment. Asked whether they feared for themselves and their children, people living there said: “Yes, we are afraid, but where can we go? This is better than staying out on the street.”

Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite the ceasefire. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025.

blocks.caption: Civil defence and municipal teams conduct search and rescue operations. Photograph: Saeed M M T Jaras/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: This year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel had continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

Separately, a video from the Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood of Gaza City showed the aftermath of an Israeli drone strike that killed Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded several other people. Al-Zinati had been trying to recover the body of a man killed in an earlier strike.
Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said on Wednesday that it was only a matter of time before Israel resumed full-scale war in Gaza and moved to force out its Palestinian population.

Katz, responding to criticism from another rightwing politician before the 27 October elections, said 70% of Gaza had already been emptied of its population during Israel’s offensive launched after the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
He added that the Israel Defense Forces were prepared “to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan”,.
Since the war began, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry.

articles.title: House votes for a third time to end Iran war in symbolic move as conflict drags on – US politics live
articles.summary: The action is likely the last House vote on issue ahead of the midterm elections

blocks.text: Key events

items: 14m agoHouse votes for a third time to end the Iran war as conflict drags on

blocks.text: House votes for a third time to end the Iran war as conflict drags on
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

For a third time, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt president Donald Trump’s ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The roll call late Tuesday, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict.
None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure, AP reported.
“Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?” said Democratic representative Seth Moulton, who served as a marine during the Iraq war and pushed the resolution forward.
He said it’s time for Congress to “actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration.”

Republican Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat.

Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending” - the decades of hostilities from Iran. “They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States,” Mast said. “Enough is enough.”
The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections, where the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns.
In other developments:

items: As part of a $2.8bn package of military aid, the Trump administration plans to send Israel a type of one-ton bombs that were withheld by the Biden administration over concerns that they were being used to kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

Donald Trump “threw a tantrum” when he heard that Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty, a trustee of the Kennedy Center whose lawsuit forced Trump’s name to be removed from the facade of the memorial, had again prevailed in court.

A televised Michigan Senate debate in Detroit on Tuesday was distinctly one-sided, because the Democratic nominee, Dr Abdul El-Sayed turned up, while his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, chose not to attend.

Todd Blanche, the US attorney general, alerted reporters at the White House to stand by for what he called “a big development” in the federal crackdown on voting by non-citizens to be announced by Ryan Raybould, the US attorney for the Northern District of Texas. When it came, however, Raybould’s announcement, that his office had charged six lawful permanent residents and one undocumented immigrant for voting in federal elections over the past eight years, hardly lived up to the billing.

articles.title: Philippines' Duterte seen in person for first time at International Criminal Court
articles.summary: He is due to be tried for crimes against humanity over thousands of deaths linked to his war on drugs.

blocks.text: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where he is due to be tried for alleged crimes against humanity.
He is facing charges over his bloody war on drugs, which saw tens of thousands of small-time drug dealers allegedly executed summarily.
The 81-year-old wore a dark suit and white shirt with no tie on Wednesday, the first time he has been seen in person since his arrest in Manila 18 months ago.
Until now he had appeared before the court by video link and subsequently skipped multiple hearings.
The ICC called a status hearing on Wednesday after Duterte's lawyers argued the former leader's deteriorating health had made him unfit to stand trial.
The first trial date is scheduled in November.
The war on drugs was the centrepiece of Duterte's presidency, which ran from 2016 to 2022. He argued peace and order was necessary to grow the economy.
The ICC is looking at killings from 1 November 2011, when Duterte was mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, to 16 March 2019, when he withdrew the Philippines' membership in the ICC.
Duterte's lawyer Peter Haynes has told the court his client suffers from "significant memory impairment", making him unable to engage with his legal team. Prosecutors argued otherwise.

In 2019, when he was still president, Duterte revealed he was suffering from myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition that causes nerve malfunction. At 71 in 2016, he was the oldest Philippine president at the time of election.

Duterte heads to trial at the ICC as his family is caught in a high-stakes dynasty war for control of the Philippines. His daughter, Vice-President Sara Duterte, has feuded spectacularly with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos.
The break-up of the Duterte-Marcos alliance, which helped them win the 2022 elections by a landslide, paved the way for the Rodrigo Duterte's arrest at Manila airport in March 2025.
Sara Duterte is a frontrunner to replace Marcos in the 2028 elections, where the incumbent is ineligible under the constitution to stand for a second term.
But she is also fighting for her political survival in an impeachment trial, where if convicted, she will be disqualified from running for public office.
She is charged with misusing public funds and threatening to have Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and Marcos' cousin, congressman Ferdinand Martin Romualdez assassinated.

articles.title: At least 19 killed, including children, as unstable Gaza building collapses
articles.summary: A building housing half a dozen families gave out in Gaza City overnight into Wednesday, killing 19 people as they slept and leaving rescuers digging through rubble for dozens more who had been…

image.caption: People gather as civil defence workers attempt to rescue those who are trapped beneath the rubble of a residential building that collapsed in Gaza City on Wednesday. (Mahmoud Issa/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A building housing half a dozen families gave out in Gaza City overnight into Wednesday, killing 19 people as they slept and leaving rescuers digging through rubble for dozens more who had been sheltering inside the structure.
Building reconstruction, repair have not taken place in Gaza since last year's ceasefire between Israel, Hamas

A building housing half a dozen families gave out in Gaza City overnight into Wednesday, killing 19 people as they slept and injuring 25, and leaving rescuers digging through rubble for dozens more who'd been sheltering inside the structure.

The sudden collapse of the building, which was known to be unstable due to damage from Israeli strikes earlier in the war, underscored how perilous and desperate living conditions have grown for the majority of the enclave's population as a ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas stalls.

The dead include at least 13 women and children, according to Zaher al-Wahidi, a spokesperson for the Gaza Health Ministry. The toll was expected to rise as more bodies were recovered from the wreckage.

All of Gaza's roughly two million people now live in a stretch of land that makes up less than half of the territory. They remain dependent on aid and are surrounded by Israeli troops who carry out strikes or attacks on a near-daily basis, with hundreds of Palestinians killed since the ceasefire was reached late last year.

items: UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
Gaza doc NAZA earns 24.5-minute standing ovation at Venice premiere

blocks.text: There's been no reconstruction work since the ceasefire. Israel has said it will not allow any rebuilding until Hamas disarms.
The level of destruction means Palestinians have been forced to choose between crowded tent camps or what's left of the enclave's damaged buildings.
'No other choice'

At least six displaced Palestinian families were living in the structure that collapsed early Wednesday despite knowing that it was teetering on the brink of collapse, according to Gaza's civil defence.
"The lack of options and alternatives left them with no other choice," said Aboud Majdalawi, a rescuer with the force.
Israel’s yellow line is moving, pushing Palestinians closer to the sea
In the aftermath of the collapse, people were searching desperately for loved ones or their remains.

A group of men were seen carrying the headless body of a child. Others sat atop a pile of rubble, pulling desperately at flashes of colour they believed could be clothing worn by a survivor. All they found were dust-caked blankets wedged in the debris.
Day 610:43A Palestinian humanitarian worker says Israel is erasing the possibility of a Palestinian state

Despite a U.S.-brokered ceasefire in October 2025 that reduced fighting in Gaza, Israel has continued to carry out strikes, as both sides accuse each other of violating the truce. At least 1,375 people have been killed since the agreement went into effect, according to local health officials.
The nearly three-year Israel-Hamas war — launched after Hamas's deadly raid into Israel in October 2023 — has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.

articles.title: US charges 5 people over Russia-backed plots
articles.summary: US prosecutors accuse the foreign nationals of conducting surveillance, attacks, and murder-for-hire operations for Moscow — just after a DW investigation identified one of the suspects as a salsa…

image.caption: The DOJ unsealed the charges one day after DW published an investigation into one of the members of the network, Oemis Romagoza DurruthyImage: LRT

blocks.text: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has charged five men with working for Russianintelligence to carry out surveillance and plan targeted killings in the United States and Europe.
"The men were recruited to carry out attacks and assassinations around the world, including the United States," the DOJ said in the indictment.

Yuri Khrameev, 63, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, both Russian nationals; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Angel Eduardo Castro of Venezuela, 22, were charged with an alleged conspiracy to commit financial terrorism.
Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire.
All the individuals are still at large.
The DOJ announced the unsealing of charges against the five individuals one day after DW published an investigation looking into one of the members of the murder plot.

The DW investigation identified Romagoza Durruthy as a salsa teacher in Russia who recruited a number of people in 2024 to carry out sabotage across Europe. The agents were mostly from Spanish-speaking countries and had been sent across Europe to commit arson attacks on businesses and military equipment destined for Ukraine. The investigation found that Romagoza Durruthy had been the person who directed them and organized their travels.
How a Cuban dance teacher aided Russian sabotage in EU
What else did the DOJ say?
Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the plans included attempts to assassinate a Russian dissident in Washington, DC.

According to the DOJ, several people were recruited in the US alone to surveil Russian dissidents, in addition to monitoring civilian and military infrastructure in European countries such as Lithuania.
The Justice Department also reported that one recruit was allegedly offered "$40,000 to 'eliminate' or 'disappear' a US resident."
Last year, another recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania. Russia has previously denied carrying out such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States.
The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
