articles.title: Von der Leyen eyes Canada as EU's first 'associate member'
articles.summary: EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU and Canada saw the world with the same eyes. At her annual State of the Union address, she said the bloc was dealing with an "openly hostile world."

image.caption: Von der Leyen said she wants Canada to be an 'associate member' of the EUImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union was opening the door for ‌Canada ⁠to ⁠become its first associate member — a position that the bloc would have to create from scratch.
Von der Leyen's comments came during her annual speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, while Candanian Prime Minister Mark Carney was in attendance.
This comes days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc, a position that does not currently exist.
Earlier this week, Carney responded to the story, saying he sought a "unique alliance"with the bloc and not a membership.

"Partnerships are a ​strategic ‌choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture ‌in the international rules-based system," ‌von ​der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union ​address.

"We see the world with the same ⁠eyes: ​from AI ​to climate change, from the Arctic ​to geopolitics. And ‌we have stood together: on Ukraine, on ​defense, ⁠on raw materials and on supply chains. ⁠But ​above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy," she said.
The EU and Canada, which have already grown close amid conflicts and trade wars, are looking to partner with each other to diversify from China and the United States respectively.
As Trump menaces, some think Canada should join the EU
Warning against an 'openly hostile world'
Von der Leyen called for an independent European Union amid an "openly hostile world," in her speech on Wednesday.

"'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' — this is how British author Charles Dickens described Europe in the days of the French Revolution, and it is also a fair description of the world we live in," she said, beginning her address.
"The state of our union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been," she said.

blocks.caption: Von der Leyen was first elected president of the European Commission in 2019 and then again in 2024Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Von der Leyen warned against "an openly hostile world" and "frayed relationships" while speaking of Russia's war against Ukraine and not directly mentioning the EU's increasingly strained relationship with the US.

"A territorial war ‌of aggression is ‌raging ​on our continent; others have erupted nearby. A ​fight for industrial capacities is shaping ⁠global ​competition. And ​a battle of ​narratives is seeking ‌to weaken confidence in ​Europe," ⁠von der Leyen said.
Von der Leyen announces new European corporation on critical raw material
Von der Leyen, now in her second five-year term as commission president, stressed on the need to maintain European independence in various sectors including energy and raw material.
"We still have too many dangerous dependencies" she said adding the EU was still 80% dependent on China for many critical raw materials.
"We need to urgently procure and build up reserves. No country can do this on its own so we need to think differently," she said, hinting at global partnerships without mentioning nations.

"This is why we will establish a new European corporation on critical raw material. It will help us obtain and stockpile what we need ... Not only our industry depends on this but also our independence and security," she said.
As for China, the president warned the bloc would "use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship".

"Our trade deficit with China is now one billion euros a day. It has reached a tipping point. Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," she said. "Words are good. But deeds are better."
Future 'depends' on how EU tackles climate change, AI
Speaking of challenges, von der Leyen said the future of the 27-nation bloc depends on how it manages climate change and artificial intelligence.

"Our future prosperity and security will greatly depend on how we manage the tipping points of our time: climate change and AI," she said, promising a new "heatwave plan" following Europe's deadly summer, and a push for the bloc to help "pace the frontier" of AI development.
Von der Leyen, a mother of seven, also proposed sweeping restrictions on children's access to social media.
Under the proposal, children under 13 would be barred from accessing such services, while those aged 13 to 15 would be allowed to use restricted "mini accounts" supervised by a parent or guardian.
"I am aware that many perceive the power of Big Tech as overwhelming and impossible to roll back. I disagree," von der Leyen said.

articles.title: How extreme weather is hurting the global economy
articles.summary: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.

image.caption: We are already paying a price for burning fossil fuelsImage: Robin Utrecht/picture alliance

blocks.text: The last 11 years have been the planet's hottest on record. This changing climate is manifested in extreme weather events like heat waves and wildfires. But less obvious are the higher prices and lower wages linked to a heating world.

According to a 2026 study by the MIT Sloan School of Management and UCLA School of Law, climate change has already driven up average American household expenses by $900 (€780) a year — rising to above $1,300 for one in 10 US counties.

These costs would not exist in a world without climate change. They include escalating home insurance ($600 higher on average), increasing state and federal taxes due to disaster recovery costs or health impacts from wildfire smoke, for example.
"Climate inaction isn't just an environmental failure; it acts like a tax on every American household," wrote the researchers .

blocks.caption: An 8-month drought in California sparked catastrophic wildfires in 2025. But heat is also burning a hole in personal wealthImage: Mike Blake/REUTERS

blocks.text: How climate change is already hitting incomes

A 2024 report by Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact estimated that climate damages to agriculture, infrastructure, health and productivity could cost the world economy $38 trillion a year by 2050.
But how have climate-driven weather extremes already impacted salaries and household budgets?

"If we can't figure out what climate change is already costing us with the data we have, projecting the future becomes almost hopeless," said Derek Lemoine, an economics professor from the University of Arizona who has estimated a 12% reduction in US incomes as global temperatures have risen. This is also compared to a non-climate change scenario.
Lemoine shows how temperature extremes in one US county are having cascading economic impacts in distant locations with milder weather due to interconnected trade and supply chains.
"Much work studies climate change as if it changes weather in only one year and one location at a time," Lemoine told DW.

Instead, he wants to understand how, if a heat wave wipes out corn crops across America, other industries that rely on that corn, including livestock and food producers, will be impacted as the commodity becomes scarcer and increases in price.

blocks.caption: Drought-affected agriculture is having compounding economics impactsImage: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: "As your costs have gone up," said Lemoine of producers impacted across the corn supply chain, "that's going to serve to make the income of everyone who depends on you go down."

Climate's impact on trade is also being felt in Germany, where record low water levels on the Rhine River, the busiest inland trade waterway in Europe, could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter of 2026, noted the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in July.

Prolonged dry weather linked to climate change is to blame as shipping capacity drops to as low as 15% on the river that connects Europe's largest port in Rotterdam in the Netherlands with much of western Germany.
Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships
Compounding existing economic pressures
One Australian study also looks at how broad climate changes, rather than local shocks from single extreme weather events have gradually led to a decrease in productivity and economic output.

Timothy Neal, a researcher at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales in Australia, co-authored the report showing that global heating reduced economic output in the state of NSW by an average of around 18%, or the equivalent of $21,288 Australian dollars (€12,974, $15,000) per person in 2024.
"The damage has already been quite severe," Neal told DW, adding that in a non-warming scenario, citizens would enjoy "lower food prices" and "lower poverty."

The report refers to droughts in parts of NSW in the mid-late 2010s that reduced productivity across the whole state by up to 10 billion Australian dollars due to lower agricultural yields and farm incomes, higher water costs and increased reliance on government assistance.
These financial impacts compounded through the state economy over time, influencing the cost of food, insurance and infrastructure maintenance.
In the words of the report, these effects also "compound existing economic pressures and contribute to widening disparities between regions," meaning an increase in income and wealth inequality.

blocks.caption: Putting planet-heating CO2 in the atmosphere is compounding economic stagnationImage: Stefan Ziese/imagebroker/IMAGO

blocks.text: Can climate adaptation limit costs?

"Climate change action should not be seen as a predominantly environmental but also economically sensible," said Frank Jotzo, an economist at the NSW Net Zero Commission, which works to decarbonize the state and commissioned the above study.

Referring to "defensive climate investments" such as reinforcing roads, railways and shipping infrastructure to adapt to a hotter world, Jotzo added that "if it wasn't for climate change, we could be putting that money and that effort into other things."
However, adaptation efforts such as the greening of cities to reduce heat island effects will be vital to head off much worse future economic impacts.
The 2026 European heat waves, for example, have already cost around €180 billion, which is the EU's entire projected economic growth for the year, according to one analysis.

Adaptation will also involve strengthening the hospital and medical system to counteract the health effects of heat waves that also reduce productivity as heat-stressed employees tire or struggle to sleep, Jotzo noted.

blocks.caption: Workers around the world are losing productivity due to extreme heatImage: Assad Hani/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: But Lemoine says that adaptation to climate-driven economic decline is so "costly in its own right" that it could exacerbate income loss and be ineffective if not done comprehensively.
Only when "all places" are insulated from weather extremes can the cascading economic impacts be addressed, he says.

Nonetheless, both adaptation and a rapid reduction of planet-heating emissions are together required to avoid climate-driven income loss that will worsen if warming outstrips Paris climate agreement targets.
"Unchecked climate change would create a permanent drain on wages and productivity," said Jotzo.
The economic cost of climate change and how to adapt

Culture secretary says X ‘didn’t even bother to turn up’ to meeting about abuse, intimidation and doxxing on social media

UK inflation has returned above 3% as soaring fuel and transport…

blocks.text: Key events

18m agoUK inflation rises to 3.1% as motor fuel prices jump by almost a quarter
32m agoLisa Nandy brands Musk’s X a ‘disgrace’ as she pledges crackdown on social media doxxing

blocks.text: Piddington, small Oxfordshire village, votes for independence in symbolic referendum in protest over migrant camp
An Oxfordshire village which could house more than 1,000 asylum seekers has voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic “referendum”, the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markThe people of Piddington have voted to secede from the UK after the government announced plans to house 1,256 male asylum seekers at a nearby former military base. Some 285 villagers backed “independence”, with a turnout of nearly 92%. Only 26 residents voted against the motion, with one spoiled ballot recorded. The result was announced by a returning officer to an audience of dozens of journalists and residents gathered outside the village hall this morning.

blocks.caption: Returning officer Susannah Parden announcing the result of the symbolic “referendum” in the village of Piddington, Oxfordshire this morning. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA
An aerial view of Piddington. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as motor fuel prices jump by almost a quarter
UK inflation has returned above 3% as soaring fuel and transport prices triggered by the Iran war heap renewed pressure on British households, Richard Partington reports.
Lisa Nandy brands Musk’s X a ‘disgrace’ as she pledges crackdown on social media doxxing

Good morning. We will be hearing from Andy Burnham today because he is back at work having taken time off following the death of his father. And already we have heard from Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, who has been doing a media round.
She has condemned Elon Musk’s social media platform, X, describing it as an “absolute disgrace”.

Nandy was talking about what social media companies are doing to stop people using their platforms to post intimidatory messages online, in particular posting private information like an address that might put someone at risk (doxxing). Yesterday Nandy hosted a meeting with social media companies about this, partly prompted by the abuse RNLI volunteers have been getting online by anti-migrant vigilantes who hate the lifeboat service for the role it plays protecting people on small boats at risk of drowning.
Speaking on Times Radio this morning, Nandy said:

double quotation markI had the social media companies in to see me yesterday to talk to them about their responsibilities in this regard. All of the different social media companies have completely different terms of service, different standards that they apply to online hatred directed at individuals. Some of them will automatically remove that content. Some of them, frankly, won’t. X didn’t even bother to turn up yesterday, which I think is an absolute disgrace.
Nandy said she was determined to stop doxxing.

double quotation markI have made a commitment to the RNLI and to, not just charities but public sector workers, police officers, and others who are being routinely harassed and abused online in the course of work, that we will tighten up the law. We will make sure that where, for example, people’s addresses are being published online, that we just do not allow that to happen, that those things will have to be either blocked or taken down immediately. We cannot have a situation where not just charity volunteers, but shop workers and social workers and police officers are being routinely harassed online in the course of their work.
I will post more from her interviews shortly.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning: Andy Burnham is visiting a factory in the south-east of England.
Late morning: Burnham meets Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general, in Oxfordshire.
11.30am: Simon Case, the former cabinet secretary, gives evidence to the Lords constitutional committee on constitutional safeguards.
12.30pm: Alex Burghart, the Tory deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, speak at Policy Exchange’s Britain and the EU: After the Reset event.
Also, during the day Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, is doing a round of interviews with regional media ahead of his party’s conference, which starts at the weekend.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Is Donald 'drill, baby, drill' Trump helping the world transition away from oil?

image.caption: Donald Trump, shown here speaking in Pennsylvania on Oct. 14, 2024, was very pro-oil on the U.S. presidential election campaign trail. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: While running for the U.S. presidency in 2024, Donald Trump promised to do almost anything to benefit the oil industry. His slogan: "Drill, baby, drill."

But his bold actions since retaking office have in many ways had the opposite effect. While oil companies rake in windfall revenues, Trump's punitive tariffs on China and the price shocks from the war he started with Iran in February have driven many countries to consider the upsides of renewable energy.

"This is Economics 101. If you increase the price of a good and make it riskier, then you will drive people to search for alternatives," said Kingsmill Bond, director of global energy think-tank Ember. "That's exactly what's been happening."

One of the most obvious examples is electric vehicles. A report released last month by the International Energy Agency (IEA) found the global EV market rebounded in the second quarter of this year, even as overall car sales declined.

Statistics collected by Ember show that EV exports from China, the world's biggest EV producer, between March-May 2025 and March-May 2026 spiked — up 117 per cent in Brazil, 127 per cent in South Korea, 175 per cent in Australia and 220 per cent in Italy.

Countries are also adapting their energy grids to the new reality. Earlier this year, the U.K.'s largest energy supplier reported a 50 per cent increase in solar panel sales, year over year, while rising energy costs in Asia have boosted rooftop solar. Even as Canada looks to expand investment in pipelines, the government has announced a nuclear strategy aimed at doubling the electrical grid's capacity by 2050.
"EVs and batteries and solar panels are flying out the door, because people want an alternative," Bond said.
Countries seeking energy security

As Bond points out, the broader energy transition has been underway for a while. In its review of 2025, for example, Ember noted that renewables produced more than one-third of global electricity generation, "overtaking coal power for the first time in 100 years."
But the Iran war gave people the world over new incentive to consider clean energy.

Iran's response to the U.S.-Israeli attacks that began in February was to block the transit of one-fifth of the world's oil through the Strait of Hormuz. As the price of oil rose to nearly $120 US a barrel, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it "the second fossil fuel crisis in just a few years," after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"There is one thing that all these events are making clear," she said. "We are paying a very high price for our overdependency on fossil fuels."
Saudi Arabia shuts key oil pipeline after drone attack launched from inside Iraq
This seems to be a lesson many countries have learned — particularly in Asia.

For example, Thailand has turned to solar in lieu of rising natural gas prices. Soon after the Iran war began, the Philippines declared an energy emergency and its government signed executive orders to speed up grid connections and a number of projects aimed at creating 1.4 gigawatts of renewable energy (roughly enough to power one million homes).

From an environmental perspective, the responses to the Iran war's energy shocks haven't all been positive; coal usage is projected to hit a record high this year, according to the IEA. Some countries that relied on natural gas have had to switch to coal as the main alternative for powering their electrical grids, due to the shipping constraints on liquid natural gas (LNG) through the Strait of Hormuz.

But in some cases, reactively reverting to cheaper and dirtier coal is happening in tandem with a proactive clean transition. Both Pakistan and the Philippines have increased their use of coal to offset some of the dependence on gas, but Pakistan's solar transition has been in the works for several years, with solar's slice of the electricity mix nearly tripling between 2023 and 2025, according to Ember.

Even as most of its LNG supply comes from Qatar, Pakistan's Power Minister Awais ‌Leghari was quick to point out how the country's uptake in renewables would cushion it from the disruptions in the Middle East, telling Reuters, "Pakistan is not expected to invest in any source of power that could put it at risk in terms of energy security."
Erica Downs, a senior research scholar at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University in New York, said electrification inevitably enhances energy security.
"What country doesn't want to be increasingly self-sufficient in energy production and supply?"

Montreal-based Northern Light Capital Partners led a study that showed that by March 30, a month after the start of the Iran war, more than 150 countries had announced they were investing in clean energy for energy security reasons.

"The U.S. administration's tariffs injected erratic volatility into clean energy supply chains," Joanna Klimczak, founder and CEO of Northern Light Capital Partners, told CBC News. "The war in Iran, meanwhile, has been a definitive accelerant for clean energy investment globally."
'A marathon, not a sprint'
The story of the renewable energy transition can't be told without highlighting China's role. It has been producing solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles at a dizzying pace.

Early in his second term, Trump slapped massive tariffs on a variety of Chinese products, including solar panels. One result is that a lot of them were redirected to Africa, where they are helping countries such as Rwanda, Senegal, Ivory Coast and even oil-rich Nigeria end their reliance on fossil fuels like diesel.

"The cost of equipment went down when the trade war started. The Chinese were desperate to offload," Fawen Nyakudya, managing director of Zimbabwe-based PFN Solar Systems, told German media outlet DW.
Klimczak says that as a result of decades of investment in clean tech manufacturing, China has been able to accommodate global demand for renewable energy at a decisive moment.

Downs points out that unlike during the oil shocks in 1973 (due to the OPEC embargo), 1979 (the Iranian revolution) and 1990 (the first Iraq war), "there are technologies that exist today that give people alternatives to fossil fuels that they wouldn't have had in decades past."
They're not only available but, in most cases, are cheaper to deploy than traditional fossil fuels.

According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, since 2010, the installed costs of solar have declined by 87 per cent, onshore wind by 55 per cent and battery storage has fallen by 93 per cent.

Downs says it's "still a little early to tell" if Trump's trade and military exploits have had a lasting impact on the global energy transition. One key question is whether the price of oil went high enough "to force a more permanent shift to clean tech."
On Monday, the price of a barrel of Brent crude hit $109 US — the highest since May. But oil has yet to reach the lofty levels some analysts predicted earlier in the year.
"Oil didn't hit $200 [a barrel] — didn't hit $150," Downs said. "I've heard some people question, is it actually not a good thing, in the long term, that prices did not reach those sky-high levels?"
The energy transition is inevitable, Bond says, and moments like this accelerate the pace.

"This is a marathon, not a sprint. There is an ongoing shift from fossil fuels to alternatives that's been going on for a long time," he said. "And every time there's a shock like this, it just encourages people [to change] a little bit faster."

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: A new bill may allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy
India and Russia energy ties have only strengthened since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Wednesday, September 16:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 16, 2026
US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India

India-US ties could come under pressure as the US lawmakers consider a Russia sanctions bill that would allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas. India, a major consumer of Russian energy, could be affected by the measure.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in a 214-211 vote, media reports said. The House is expected to hold a final vote on Wednesday.
The bill, imposing sanctions on Russia's leadership, energy and defense sectors and "shadow fleet" accused of helping Moscow evade oil sanctions, was passed by the Senate last month.
If approved by the House, the bill would go to Trump to be signed into law.
The proposed tariffs seek toincrease economic pressure on Moscow by targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy.
India-US ties facing test

While India and Russia ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports, the same cannot be said of India-US relations under Prime Minister Narendra Modi as tensions mounted over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil.
Last August, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports over those purchases, on top of a 25% reciprocal tariff.
However, the additional Russia-related tariff was removed in February 2026, while the reciprocal tariff was reduced to 18% as part of a US-India trade framework.
However, the landmark bilateral trade agreement between the two countries remains in limbo, with no significant breakthrough.

articles.title: Cases stuck in limbo, detainees pleading guilty over justice system delays in northern Quebec
articles.summary: Nunavik’s travelling court — which services several of the fly-in only northern communities on rotation — cancelled in-person fall dates in both Inukjuak and Puvirnituq, primarily due to the lack of…

image.caption: Advocates say the delays are leading some detainees to opt for a guilty plea and impacting the accused’s right to be tried in a reasonable time. (CBC News Graphics)

blocks.text: It’s been nine months since Andrew Naluktuk was home or saw his family following a police-involved shooting in northern Quebec that led to the death of his six-year-old daughter.
Since then, he’s been waiting — in detention — about 1,000 kilometres away from his family in Inukjuak.
His court date was supposed to be in August. But August became September — and September’s date was pushed to December.
Exceptionally, his lawyer pushed for an online court date scheduled for this Thursday, according to a family spokesperson.
The delays come after Nunavik's travelling court — which serves several fly-in northern communities on rotation — cancelled in-person court dates this fall in Inukjuak and Puvirnituq.
It’s primarily due to the lack of necessary accommodation for those involved in the cases, says lawyer Lucie Demers, the executive assistant to the Court of Quebec Chief Judge Henri Richard.

While the Court of Quebec, which operates the travelling court, was unable to confirm how many cases are affected by this delay, activities should “in principle” resume in January 2027, said Demers in an emailed statement to CBC News.
But advocates say the long wait is leading some to opt for a guilty plea and impacting the accused’s right to be tried in a reasonable time.
“There's something wrong here,” said Sarah Ruptash, Naluktuk’s aunt, who is speaking out on behalf of his family.
“It does not help a person heal while being held in the cell. Mentally, it must be excruciating.”

Naluktuk is facing charges for weapons possession, assault, assault of a peace officer, and unlawfully causing bodily harm to a child. He is also facing charges for discharging a firearm with intent, pointing a firearm and possession contrary to order.
‘It's been so long,’ says family member
It’s difficult for Ruptash to talk about the last time she saw her nephew and his daughter.
Following the incident, the two were sent to the local health centre in Inukjuak before getting transferred south to hospitals for further medical treatment.
“I broke down,” recalled Ruptash. “I couldn't sleep afterwards. Why should that child be in this situation?”

According to a statement released by Quebec’s police watchdog, officers with the Nunavik Police Service were called to a home in the early morning of Dec. 20, 2025, following reports of a person who posed a danger to other occupants.
Police officers arrived on the scene, encountered a person with a firearm outside the residence and an exchange of gunfire reportedly ensued.

According to the statement, an individual was injured in the intervention, arrested and taken to hospital in stable condition while another person was reportedly found seriously injured inside the home and was later transported to hospital.

items: Man appears in court in connection with shootout involving police in Inukjuak, Que.

blocks.text: Ten days after the incident, the BEI confirmed the seriously injured person – identified as the six-year-old girl by local authorities – had died.
Ruptash says this whole ordeal has been very hard on the family and on her nephew. She was particularly disheartened when he was denied bail in April.
“It was heartbreaking enough for him to lose his daughter,” she said.
“He calls me once in a while. I tried to let him know that the time will come when he'll be released, but it's been so long.”
Some suspects pleading guilty due to delays

Detention is hard on anyone, says lawyer Virginie Dallaire, but especially for Inuit — who are flown out of their communities and held in facilities in Amos or Saint-Jérôme, Que., hundreds of kilometres from home, family and resources.
“Any period of detention is much harsher,” said Dallaire, a defence lawyer with Yves Ménard Avocats, who takes on cases in northern communities, mainly on the Hudson Bay coast.
“But now, with that unknown and having to wait months and months… it’s just extremely difficult.”

items: In Quebec's north, criminal cases are being dropped because of a drastic lack of resources

blocks.text: Current delays for the fall dates are leading some of Dallaire’s clients to change their pleas — to guilty, she says.
“A lot of them that had initially asked for trial contacted us saying, ‘I'm not going to wait [until] 2027. I want a deal,’” she said.

The Court of Quebec noted it has adopted a declaration and a reconciliation action plan to make justice among Indigenous people a priority, “notably that which concerns activities of the travelling court,” read its statement.

To reduce the impact of this situation, the court says it has put in place various measures, including progressing cases and in some circumstances, not requiring in-person sessions. It says it has also met with representatives and mayors of villages to come up with solutions.
But Suzy Kauki, a justice advocate in Nunavik, says things keep changing without the communities’ knowledge.
“Here we go again,” she said. “More changes being made for the community without the community.”
Kauki, who previously worked in suicide prevention, began studying the justice system in Nunavik.

The way things are — with all the postponements and the cancellations — she says some can feel forced to plead guilty “without really understanding what pleading guilty is going to mean 10 years from now,” she said.
“The heaviest systemic racism that we face in the north right now is within the justice system and the health system,” she said.

The office of Quebec's minister responsible for relations with the First Nations and the Inuit, Ian Lafrenière, said he was “sensitive” to the situation, but did not provide a comment to CBC News. His office instead referred CBC to the Justice Ministry.
The office of Quebec Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barette did not respond to CBC in time for publication.

Johanne Fortin, the director of legal, social, judicial and municipal management department for the Kativik Regional Government, acknowledged "the gravity of the situation," noting lack of accommodation is not just a problem for the travelling court.
Hotel rooms in Nunavik ‘always full’

Mark Blair, general manager of the Fédération des coopératives du Nouveau-Québec (FCNQ-Ilagiisaq), says Nunavik has 282 hotel rooms across 13 communities, but the region needs to double its capacity to answer the current and future need.
“They're booked all the time. They're always full,” he said.
The federation provides hotel training, support and manages booking for the independent co-operative hotels across Nunavik.

But with the cost of construction in the north dramatically increasing since the COVID-19 pandemic, it would cost an estimated $203.6 million to add 275 rooms to the existing 13 independent co-operative hotels, he says.
These hotels, he notes, offer essential services to the community — with its primary clientele being government services, including the courts, health, education and social services workers.

items: An Inuk's fight for a new justice system in northern Quebec

blocks.text: Typically, the courts book at the start of the year, after their schedule is determined. But Blair says this year, they were only informed of the schedule at the end of April or beginning of May.
“We just got it way too late and the hotels were already filled," he said.
Considering the longstanding issue with accommodation, this problem could have been predicted by the travelling court, says lawyer Dallaire.
The extent of this delay is unjustified and “truly a lack of respect,” she said.
“Whether it's for the accuser, the witness or the victim in the case,” said Dallaire.
The more the case is delayed, the more time separates the accused, the victim and witnesses from the alleged incident, she notes.

“Your memory needs to be fresh so that you can defend yourself,” she said. “And the more we drag this justice, it's injustice for the client, it's injustice for the witness, for the victim, for everyone.”

articles.title: This was the last lake of its kind in Canada. Now it's gone.
articles.summary: Canada's last epishelf lake — made up of freshwater floating on saltwater — is gone, along with the unique ecosystem it supported, scientists confirm. Here's what made the lake special, and what it…

image.caption: Jérémie Bonneau tries to free a probe called a mooring from the ice of the Milne Fiord epishelf lake in 2018. The lake was ice-covered year-round and was the last of its kind in Canada until it drained into the ocean in 2020. (Yulia Antropova/Water and Ice Research Laboratory/Carleton University)

blocks.text: Science·New

Canada's last epishelf lake — made up of freshwater floating on saltwater — is gone, along with the unique ecosystem it supported, scientists confirm. Here's what made the lake special, and what it disappearance says about the transformation of the Arctic in a warming climate.
In a polar epishelf lake, freshwater floats on seawater, creating a unique ecosystem
Canada's only remaining epishelf lake — made up of freshwater floating on saltwater — is gone, along with the unique ecosystem it supported, scientists confirmed in a new study.

Jérémie Bonneau, the lead author and an assistant professor at Laval University in Quebec City, said its loss is sad, as the Milne Fiord epishelf lake on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut was "the last thing like that in Canada."
"Suddenly, it's … drained away and then everything that was living in there is gone."
Bonneau noted that the complete disappearance of a once common phenomenon shows how a warming climate is transforming the Arctic.

While scientists had previously reported the lake's demise, the new study, recently published in the journal Scientific Reports, details how it happened and says the irreversible loss "marks a regime shift and the end of a 4000-year era."
Major ice shelf lake in Canada has disappeared
How epishelf lakes form
Glaciers are rivers of ice. Typically, they flow into the sea, and so does any meltwater on their surface. Normally, that freshwater is quickly mixed into the seawater by wind and waves.
But the mouth of Milne Fiord has been dammed for thousands of years by the Milne Ice Shelf — a huge, flat piece of ice sitting on the ocean and attached to the north shore of Ellsemere Island.

The dam stopped freshwater from flowing into the ocean, allowing it to accumulate on top of the saltwater of the Arctic Ocean. It formed a floating layer because freshwater is less dense than saltwater.

Meanwhile, a layer of ice about 50 to 100 centimetres thick covered the lake year-round, protecting the freshwater and saltwater layers from winds that could have mixed them together — and making the lake invisible from the surface.
Bonneau said there's evidence the lake in Milne Fiord had existed and been accumulating freshwater for more than 4,000 years.

When researchers first measured it in 1983, its freshwater layer was 18 metres deep, said Andrew Hamilton, a University of Alberta researcher who co-authored the new study. That's similar to the height of a six-storey building.

While some epishelf lakes sit completely on top of an ice shelf — that's what epishelf means — the Milne Fiord epishelf lake was actually connected to the ocean by an under-ice channel in the ice shelf, which has been thinning for about a century.
A unique ecosystem

By looking at the bacteria, viruses and phytoplankton in the two layers of the lake, researchers discovered practically no overlap between the freshwater and saltwater communities living just 20 centimetres apart.
Bonneau said, "It's really two unique ecosystems in the same water column, and you don't get that anywhere else."

Mary Thaler, who previously analyzed water from the lake for DNA but was not involved in the new study, said that while humans or fish could easily swim across the invisible border between the fresh and saltwater, for single-celled organisms, it's "an unbreakable barrier."

Analysis by Thaler and her colleagues at Laval University found bacteria and more complex eukaryotic microbes, whose cells are similar to those of plants and animals, as well as viruses. They included species that usually live in sediments on the bottom rather than in the water itself. Some of the microbes found in the lake had never previously been reported in the Arctic.

But the lake also had an influence beyond its own borders. Hamilton sent a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) into the channel in the ice shelf, where freshwater flowed out of the lake, mixed with saltwater along the way and carried nutrients to a lower depth than they would otherwise be found.
It recorded video footage of ghostly sea anemones, scallops and sea stars thriving in complete darkness below 10 metres of ice, fed by the nutrients draining from the epishelf lake.
"We were absolutely astounded to find a full, flourishing ecosystem existing within kind of this ice channel," he said.
How the lake – and its inhabitants – met their end
Then, in 2020, the Milne Ice Shelf broke into pieces off the coast of Ellesmere Island, and its wall no longer held the lake in.
Reverberations of the Milne Ice Shelf collapse
The new study looks at what happened to the ice and the lake itself before and after the collapse.
The researchers had probes called moorings that ran from the floor of the fiord to the surface, measuring salinity at different depths.
They showed that within two months of the ice shelf breaking up, the freshwater had drained and none was left in the fiord.
Thaler said freshwater organisms living there would have died more or less instantly when mixed with seawater.

While the freshwater lake was ice-covered year-round, the saltwater fiord is ice-free for part of the summer, allowing it to warm and be mixed by wind and waves — a typical marine environment suitable for organisms different from those supported by the former lake.
"And so you kind of start to see this huge change," Bonneau said.
While epishelf lakes are now completely gone from Canada, a few still exist in Greenland and Antarctica.

"Unfortunately," Hamilton said, "I think their days are numbered…. This kind of highlights that we are on a one-way trip for some of these really astounding ecosystems that make up the beauty of our planet."

articles.title: G'day, USA: Why is the U.S. accelerating military ties with Australia?
articles.summary: The U.S. may be trade-warring with Canada but it's deepening its military ties with an ally Down Under. Australia's government says that in China, it's facing "the biggest conventional military…

image.caption: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, right, was all smiles hosting Australian Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles at the Pentagon on Sept. 2. (Air Force Staff Sgt. Eugene Oliver)

blocks.text: World

The U.S. may be trade-warring with Canada but it's deepening its military ties with an ally Down Under. Australia's government says that in China, it's facing "the biggest conventional military buildup by any country in the world since the Second World War," and it wants America's help.
Increasingly powerful China is uniting 2 old allies in the Pacific
A handshake, a hug and a laugh was how U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth greeted Australia’s Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles at the Pentagon earlier this month.
Hegseth also gave the media a thumbs-up before the pair sat down for one of their now-regular meetings.
During his opening remarks, Hegseth called the event a "reflection of the deepening partnership ... at a personal level between our administrations, between our countries, between our militaries."

The high-level talks ended with a declaration that the U.S. would accelerate its military presence in Australia — which already includes a remote desert intelligence base and annual rotations of thousands of U.S. troops across Australian bases.
The U.S. remains Australia’s closest ally and principal strategic partner, said Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in a statement a few days after the meeting.

For Canadians, seeing Hegseth and Vice-President JD Vance embrace Australia at the Pentagon — and in tweets — while the U.S. administration targets this country's economy, military and sovereignty might be infuriating.
But analysts say there is a transactional tone to the tightening U.S.-Australia alliance — one that's partly explained by geography.

"Australia enables the United States to have force projection through the Indian Ocean and allows quick and easy access up through to the South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait," said James Curran, a professor of modern history at Sydney University.
In other words, two waterways China has made no secret of wanting to control.
Defensible alliance?
The timing of the meeting wasn’t accidental, as the two nations mark the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS Treaty, a security agreement between Australia, New Zealand and the U.S.
That military alliance began in 1941, when the first American soldiers landed in the state of Queensland.
"A million American service personnel used Australia as a base to project north and win the Second World War in the Pacific theatre," Marles said during the recent summit.
But Curran says that as China continues to build up its economic and military power throughout the Pacific, people at the Pentagon are realizing the U.S. position in Asia is at risk of slipping.
Australia is a strategic and sizeable outpost for the U.S. in the region and a significant complement to its network of bases in its Indo-Pacific Command.
China launches military drills, putting Taiwan on alert
For the Australian government, the prospect of increasing Chinese naval power in its waters and maritime trade corridors feels closer than ever.
The People's Liberation Army, the military wing of the Chinese Communist Party, boasts the world's largest navy and an increasingly capable long-range air force.

A 2026 report by the non-partisan think-tank the Lowy Institute found that China could strike northern Australia with ballistic missiles from its South China Sea outposts. The report's authors said this capacity would "grow substantially over the coming decade" and that China's influence might also be felt with trade disruption, the severing of undersea communication infrastructure and sophisticated cyber operations.
It's "the biggest conventional military buildup by any country in the world since the Second World War," Marles told journalists after the meeting at the Pentagon.

China remains an important trading partner for Australia, but the continued scaling up of weapons and capabilities in Australia's backyard without diplomatic efforts is concerning, Marles told a defence summit audience in 2025.
"None of that provides strategic reassurance," he said.

The reality is that over the years, Australia has had to come to terms with being a long way from its traditional allies, Curran says. The British military withdrew from the region in the late 1960s, but the Americans remained.

"Now we're looking at Chinese industrial, military and economic power at such a scale that before too long, China will become the dominant power in Asia," he said. "Does Australia, therefore, have to face the region alone for the first time in its history?"
Watching a trade war from afar
As the U.S. takes a renewed interest in Australia, the media Down Under are also paying close attention to the escalating trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

During the U.S. visit, a reporter asked Australia's deputy prime minister to justify a closer alignment with the U.S. given a recent survey highlighting a "large group of Australians who have major concerns about the reliability of the U.S. as an ally."
The U.S.-Australia alliance is justifiable, Marles said, because of the huge threat posed by China.
"This is fundamentally important to the defence of Australia," he said.
The Australian Defence Force felt that threat in 2025, when three Chinese warships were spotted sailing less than 300 kilometres off the coast of Sydney, as reported by ABC News.

Starting next year, the alliance with the U.S. will bring a rotation of U.S. nuclear-powered submarines, via a trilateral security partnership that includes the U.K. (AUKUS). Australia hopes that will eventually lead to the acquisition of its own submarines from the U.S., which are only sold to approved allies.
Referring to the alliance with the U.S., Marles said, "we are really grateful for it."
On home soil, the Australian government has been forced to defend these deepening U.S. ties.
The AUKUS alliance is under renewed scrutiny in the form of a public inquiry examining the cost, sustainability and public support of a deal that critics say was made in secrecy.

Reporting by the Guardian newspaper in Australia in September drew attention to dozens of facilities on Australia's mainland that the U.S. partially or fully controls. Figures were presented in Parliament to Australia's Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong by another senator, who claimed the U.S. has made Australia a forward operating base and exposed its citizens to retribution for U.S. foreign policy decisions.
Minister Wong rejected the claim, saying the U.S. military's presence in Australia is on a rotational basis, mutually determined and at Australia's invitation.
"We are of the view that the U.S. alliance contributes to Australian sovereignty. It enables us to have access to a range of capability that Australia would not have access to," Wong said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Georgie Smyth is a CBC Network Reporter and Producer in Vancouver. She's worked for BBC World News in London and for Nine News in Australia. She's focused on local, national and international stories that affect all Canadians. Got an idea or story tip? Email: georgina.smyth@cbc.ca

articles.title: 'Nobody wanted it to end': Seniors prom brings together long-term care residents, Brock University students
articles.summary: Their high school days might be in the rearview mirror, but residents of four long-term care homes in Ontario's Niagara region got to feel as if they were fresh-faced teenagers again, at a prom for…

image.caption: Brock University students handed roses to long-term care residents at a seniors prom at Linhaven long-term care home in St. Catharines, Ont., on Saturday. The event was part of the Brock Cares community outreach program, and featured dancing, food and intergenerational bonding. (Stephen Leithwood ph

blocks.text: Hamilton

Their high school days might be in the rearview mirror, but residents of four long-term care homes in Ontario's Niagara region got to feel as if they were fresh-faced teenagers again, at a prom for seniors held in collaboration with Brock University students.
Intergenerational event at Linhaven an emotional one for residents

Their high school days might be in the rearview mirror, but residents of four long-term care homes in Ontario's Niagara region got to feel as if they were fresh-faced teenagers again, just like they were half a century ago or longer.
Residents at the special seniors prom even got to party with Brock University students at Linhaven long-term care home in St. Catharines.
The seniors prom had all the fixings of a high school one —balloons, food, music and dancing, minus the teenage angst and someone trying to spike the punch bowl.
When we started to plan this, talking to our residents, a lot of them were saying they never attended their proms. It was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.- Heather Wild, Linhaven program manager
The intergenerational event was a huge hit, so much so that the afternoon prom went longer than it was supposed to.
"Nobody wanted it to end," said Heather Wild, program manager at Linhaven.

Residents from the three other long-term care homes operated by Niagara's regional government — Rapelje Lodge in Welland, Northland Pointe in Port Colborne and Woodlands of Sunset on the border of Welland and Pelham — were bused to the prom.
Prom was part of Brock Cares outreach

In all, more than 60 residents, some of family members and 25 Brock students were at the Linhaven prom, among a number of events that the university students volunteered to go to across Niagara on Saturday as part of the Brock Cares community outreach program.
For Emily Poole, a third-year concurrent education student, it was her third year as a Brock Cares volunteer. When she heard about the seniors prom, she couldn't miss it.
"The event was full of energy. The turnout was amazing."
Poole said it was heart-warming to see the residents get dressed up in formal attire with prom-like dresses and suits. There was even someone on site doing hair and makeup.
Wild said it was the first such event held in collaboration with Brock Cares, plus a first for many of the long-term care residents.
"When we started to plan this, talking to our residents, a lot of them were saying they never attended their proms," she said. "It was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity."
Poole volunteered in the photo booth, taking residents' photos with "silly" props.
"It was great to see their personalities shine and their excitement grow," she said, calling it "incredibly rewarding."

With a backdrop of white, gold and black balloons, and a disco ball twinkling overhead, residents satiated their sweet tooth with treats such as brownies, and custard with Linhaven Prom 2026 written with powdered chocolate on the creamy treat.
The students handed a rose to each woman.

items: University of Sask. physical therapy students start volunteer program at care home to walk seniors

blocks.text: Wild said the dance floor was hopping, first with some oldies but goodies, and then with residents' requests to the DJ.
"Some wedding songs were requested," she said. "That made it very special because it was very personal to the residents.
"There were residents and some family members who were very emotional. There were some tears."
Brock students are scheduled to return to Linhaven in the fall to help with Halloween and Thanksgiving events, Wild said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.

articles.title: At least 12 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses
articles.summary: Dozens of people are missing beneath the rubble of the building in Gaza City, where 10 families had reportedly been living.

blocks.text: At least 12 people have been killed, including children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip, according to local rescue teams.
Video footage shows the search for bodies and survivors continuing in the rubble of the multi-storey building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, its floors sandwiched together.
Locals said 10 families had been living in the apartments despite warnings that they were unsafe.

Members of the Hamas-run Civil Defence rescue service said they had initially been working with "empty hands" due to tight Israeli restrictions on equipment allowed into Gaza. However, they have since been able to borrow some heavy machinery.
On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes in Gaza killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.
The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.
Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza.

articles.title: Kosovo ex-president Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
articles.summary: A Hague tribunal ruled that Hashim Thaci, a former leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), is responsible for war crimes carried out during the war of independence with Serbia.

image.caption: Hashim Thaci, 58, had said he expected an acquittal Image: Jerry Lampen/Reuters

blocks.text: A Kosovo war crimes tribunal on Wednesday found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998-1999 war for independence from Serbia.
Thaci, a former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commander, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention.
He was tried along with three other former KLA guerrilla leaders in The Hague.
What did the tribunal rule?

The tribunal said Thaci was guilty of the murder of of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces at the hands of the KLA during the conflict. He was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people and torturing more than 300 people
The court added Thaci had "actively participated in and encouraged crimes."
Prosecutors alleged KLA forces killed more than 100 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces during and just after the Kosovo war.
This included prisoners held at KLA facilities in Kosovo and Albania, along with politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.
The defense argued that the senior KLA figures could not control or be held responsible for such acts, as the group lacked a strict command structure.
Lawyers had argued there was no direct evidence linking Thaci's command to any of the alleged crimes.
Seen as heroes in Kosovo

The accused are revered as national heroes in Kosovo, and the KLA and Thaci are seen as symbols of the independence movement. Thaci remained a central political figure after the war and was instrumental in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia.
The verdict in The Hague was livestreamed in the Kosovo capital, Pristina, where thousands of Thaci and KLA supporters gathered.
This follows rallies over the weekend that drew tens of thousands calling for the men's acquittal.
Foreign embassies warned of the possibility of unrest after the verdict.

blocks.caption: KLA supporters rallied in Pristina over the weekendImage: Zana Cimili/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Our war was just, a war of liberation," Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said ahead of the verdict.
"We believe and hope … that the KLA leaders will return free to their country and to their families," he added.
After being indicted in 2020,Thaci resigned as president and has been detained in The Hague since then.
Tribunal deeply unpopular in Kosovo
Throughout the proceedings, prosecutors tried to distinguish between Kosovo's struggle for independence from Serbia and the alleged crimes committed by the men on trial.

The tribunal responsible for prosecuting the case, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), was set up in 2016 after earlier cases in Kosovo failed due to alleged political interference and witness intimidation.
Explainer: What are the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?
Although based in The Hague, and staffed by international judges, the KSC was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged KLA war crimes.
Nevertheless, the KSC remains deeply unpopular in Kosovo. Out of 15 people indicted so far by the KSC, three are serving sentences.

"Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice," Thaci told judges in February as the proceedings concluded.

articles.title: Von der Leyen sets out challenges and opportunities for EU in ‘state of the Union’ speech – Europe live
articles.summary:
European Commission president sets out opportunities and challenges facing the European Union

Von der Leyen frames it as a choice between “independent Europe that stands up…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 3m agoEU's trade relationship with China 'unsustainable' and need to be rebalanced, von der Leyen says
5m ago'We need to electrify Europe,' von der Leyen says, to cut fossil fuel costs down
10m agovon der Leyen warns against anti-European ultranationalists and Russia who 'despise our values'
12m ago'We are now dealing with an openly hostile world,' EU's von der Leyen warns
14m agoEU 'the strongest' but 'most precarious' it has even been, von der Leyen says
36m agoWatch von der Leyen's SOTU live - video
37m agoMorning opening: The state of the European Union

blocks.text: Von der Leyen then turns to investment and growth, as well as the EU’s next budget.
She talks about the need to simplify and tackle fragmentation on investment to help fund European start ups.

She pays specific tribute to the success of ICEYE, a radar satellite imaging and space-based monitoring company, built by Finland’s Pekka Laurila and Poland’s Rafał Modrzewski after they met through Erasmus student exchange programme 15 years ago.
“Today they are one of the world’s leading space technology companies,” she says. “You are a true European success story.”
EU's trade relationship with China 'unsustainable' and need to be rebalanced, von der Leyen says
Von der Leyen turns specifically to China, warning that the EU’s trade deficit with China is now €1bn a day, and it has “reached its tipping point.”

“Some say the second China shock is looming, but it’s already here. It shows in our communities and factories across our union. It leads to deindustrialisation in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable.”
She says the EU “will use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationships.”
She also talks about the need to diversify on critical raw materials.
'We need to electrify Europe,' von der Leyen says, to cut fossil fuel costs down
Von der Leyen also talks about the need to reform Europe’s energy market.
She says “Europe cannot remain an industrial powerhouse if its energy prices are structurally too high.”

She says the bloc successfully pivoted towards homegrown cleaner energies in the aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion on Ukraine, but it still “bitterly felt the cost” of the strait of Hormuz closing later.

“We need to double down on our affordable and home-grown clean energy. Be it renewables or nuclear, be it biomethane or others. Technologically neutral. But these energies must give us independence and drive down energy prices.”
She says “we need to electrify Europe,” and cut the fossil fuel import bill.
She says lots of renewable capacity is waiting to be connected, and the EU needs to speed up grid connections.
She then turns to trade.
Von der Leyen says “kickstarting Europe’s economy is our number one priority,” as Europe needs to tap into its huge market, world class industries and services.
She says its single market remains too fragmented and needs to reform further, with the aim of completing it by the end of next year.

“In today’s economy, speed is of the essence. A permanent permit or a form, a grid connection of financing decision – all of this can determine where an investment is made and where jobs are created. We need to move much faster,” she says.
Von der Leyen also talks about the need to simplify its rules.
von der Leyen warns against anti-European ultranationalists and Russia who 'despise our values'
Von der Leyen frames it as a choice between “independent Europe that stands up for its values in this world,” or “letting divisions and dependencies hold us back.”

“Do we want to rally around our European idea that together we can decide our own destiny? Or do we let our democracies be undermined by the proxies and puppets of authoritarians? Whether it is the ultra nationalist or the anti-European, whether it’s Russian interference or disinformation, the names may be different, but their goal is the same. They despise our values and they want to shatter our European unity. So let’s not only fight back against that, but let’s fight together for our European ideal.”
'We are now dealing with an openly hostile world,' EU's von der Leyen warns
Von der Leyen warns that “we are now dealing with an openly hostile world,” in which “old assumptions and relationships have frayed.”
She talks about “a territorial war of aggression” in Ukraine, “a fight for industrial capacities” and “narratives,” and “the dizzying speech of change and technology” impacting people’s lives.

“We see this in the rise of the extreme and the decline of nuance, even in the way that we relate to each other. These real concerns are being weaponised to drive a wedge between us, sometimes from the outside, but too often from the inside. But our path is clear. Building an independent Europe that has the power to act. Nothing can divert us from this. Because in this world, the fate of Europe must remain in the hands of Europeans.”
EU 'the strongest' but 'most precarious' it has even been, von der Leyen says
Von der Leyen begins her speech.
She quotes Charles Dickens’s description of the days of the French Revolution, “it was the best of times; it was the worst of times.”
“It is also a fair description of the world we live in,” she says, as she adds “the speed of change is incredible.”

“I would say the state of our union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been. These two statements may seem incompatible, but they are both true and they reflect these exceptional times.”
She says Europe “has chosen to forge its own path” as it navigates “the complex age of … great possibilities and … great perils.”
Europe is “breaking free from the toxic dependency on Russian fossil fuels,” better prepared to defend itself than ever before, and standing for its values with Ukraine and Greenland, she says.
“In the cold fragility of today’s world, only Europe can provide true sovereignty for Europeans,” she says.
EP’s Metsola sets out what people expect from Europe:

“Our union has always moved forward because people were willing to take a leap where the moment demanded it and turned uncertainty into possibility. People expect a union that does more to protect them, more to support them, and more to fight their corner. They want answers on security, on competitiveness, on affordable homes, on quality jobs, on climate, on borders. They want us to stand up for a Europe of values …”
She goes on, also pointedly mentioning the need to continue supporting Ukraine.
Opening the session, the European parliament president Roberta Metsola welcomes Canada’s Carney, who gets long and warm applause from EU lawmakers.
“They haven’t heard you giving your speech yet,” laughs Metsola.
We are about to start.

blocks.caption: Prime minister Mark Carney participates in a welcoming ceremony with President of the European Parliament Roberta Metsola and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: It’s also worth noting that this year’s SOTU will see a special guests in attendance: Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney.

blocks.caption: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney is welcomed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and Roberta Metsola, President of the European Parliament. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters

blocks.text: He will listen to von der Leyen’s speech as Canada seeks closer ties with the EU – particularly on defence, digital regulation and trade - amid growing tensions with and outright repeated threats from US president Donald Trump.
Carney will also address the European parliament on Thursday.
Watch von der Leyen's SOTU live - video
The speech is expected to start in the next 10-15 minutes, so you can watch as the European Parliament’s Hemicycle in Strasbourg is filling up ahead of the speech.
Here’s our live stream for today:
Morning opening: The state of the European Union

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is about to speak at the European parliament to discuss “the state of the Union” in her annual speech about the EU’s place in the ever more complicated world.

blocks.caption: A light illumination on a wall at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPA

blocks.text: Her speech in Strasbourg comes as the list of challenges facing the bloc grows ever longer – not least an increasingly aggressive Russia following incidents involving Denmark, Lithuania, and Poland this week. Security is set to be a key theme.

We are also likely to hear about Europe’s competitiveness and its standing in a global race dominated by superpowers like China and the US, as well as the rise of nationalism and populism across the continent and beyond.

Expect updates on other major priorities, too: digital regulation (with a sharp focus on online safety), migration (following the Ceuta crisis in late July), and climate and energy in the wake of another record-breaking summer.
Plenty to cover. I will bring you all the key lines here.
It’s Wednesday, 16 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
